docs.t: Translating Business Problems into Claude Solutions
docs.x: A business request rarely arrives as a specification. It arrives as "we want AI to handle our claims inbox" or "can Claude help our analysts with quarterly reports". Your job as the architect is to turn that sentence into a design that someone can build, fund and defend. The exam tests whether you do that in the right order: understand the work, test it against what a model can and cannot do, and only then choose technology.

docs.h: Start from four properties of a language model
docs.c: Fluent is not the same as correct
docs.x: Every feasibility question comes back to four properties. Each one is a strength with a matching weakness, and each weakness has a standard design answer. Property Where Claude is strong Where it is weak How the design compensates Next-token prediction Summarizing, rewriting, explaining, classifying Precise specifics: names, dates, figures, citations can be plausible and wrong Citations, verification steps, tool calls to the system of record Training knowledge Common, well-documented topics Rare, recent, contested or fast-changing facts, stated with the same confidence Retrieval, web search, tools or MCP servers as the source of truth Working memory Anything inside the context window Nothing outside the window exists for the model Chunking, progressive loading, summarizing across turns Steerability Clear, concrete, checkable instructions Vague goals, long chains of logic, exact arithmetic Explicit system prompts, structured outputs, code for calculations Use the table as a checklist. For each capability the request needs, ask which property it leans on and whether the weakness matters here. If a wrong value would cost money, breach a rule or mislead a customer, the value must come from an authoritative system or a deterministic calculation, not from the model's own output. Claude can draft the sentence; the account balance comes from the banking API.

docs.t: Translating Business Problems into Claude Solutions
docs.x: A reliable sequence keeps the conversation grounded: 1. Requirement to capabilities. List what the system must actually do: read a scanned form, check a policy, draft a reply, update a record. 2. Capabilities to a sketch. Assign each capability to Claude, to an existing system or to a person (lesson 1.5 covers this split in depth). 3. Sketch to boundary conditions. Write down the limits the design depends on: document length, request volume, latency target, accuracy threshold, data that may not leave a region. 4. Boundary conditions to scope. The conditions become part of the agreed scope, so everyone knows what the system is and is not built to handle.

docs.t: Translating Business Problems into Claude Solutions
docs.h: Size it before anyone writes code
docs.x: A rough cost and latency model belongs in the feasibility stage. It needs four inputs: call volume (from the business owner, not a guess), tokens per request (input and output, as a distribution rather than an average), the model tier, and a sensitivity check (what happens if volume doubles or long documents become common). If the projection breaks the budget or the latency target, the architecture changes now, while it is still cheap to change.

docs.c: A market-briefing assistant · Choosing the technology before the constraints · Assuming the model already knows
docs.x: Verdict Meaning What you record Feasible as scoped Every capability fits the model's strengths or has a standard compensating control; cost and latency fit The assumptions, because the verdict changes if they do Feasible with constraints It works only under conditions that must be enforced, such as a document size limit or a human review gate Each constraint and what fails if it is broken Not feasible A limitation cannot be compensated within budget or scope The disqualifying constraint, and any scope reduction that would change the answer "Not feasible" is a legitimate, valuable answer. It prevents a far more expensive failure later, and naming the scope change that would make it feasible gives the business owner a real choice. An investment team wants daily briefings on current market conditions. Summarizing the analysts' own reports is a strength. Knowing today's prices is a weakness of training knowledge, so the design must bring live data in through a tool or feed. With that data source and a review step for anything sent to clients, the verdict is "feasible with constraints". Without it, the request is not feasible as scoped, however capable the model. Answers that jump straight to "use an agent" or "fine-tune a model" before volume, latency, error cost and data rules are known are usually wrong. The verdict is only as good as the constraints gathered before it. Options that rely on Claude's training data for current prices, live inventory, a customer's order or an internal policy are distractors. Anything that must be current or authoritative is brought into context at run time.

docs.t: Translating Business Problems into Claude Solutions
docs.x: Expect a short business scenario followed by four designs. The correct option typically: - keeps authoritative values (balances, prices, eligibility, order status) in the systems that own them; - uses Claude for the language work: reading, extracting, classifying, drafting, explaining; - adds a person where a wrong answer is costly or irreversible; - matches the verdict to the evidence, including "feasible with constraints" or "not feasible" when a hard limit applies. Distractors tend to over-assign work to the model, ignore a stated constraint such as a latency target or data residency rule, or choose the most powerful option without checking whether it is needed.

docs.h: Apply it: Write a feasibility brief
docs.x: Prairie State Mutual's VP of Claims Operations asks: "Can Claude take over claims intake?" Write a one-page feasibility brief that answers the question with evidence rather than enthusiasm. Use only the facts in the case. 1. Quantify today. State the current cost of intake in business units: handler hours a month, the cost of keying errors, and the SLA gap. Why: a verdict without a baseline cannot be defended, and the value case in lesson 1.6 starts from these numbers. Done when: you have three numbers, each with its unit and the case fact it comes from. 2. Check each capability against the four properties. List the capabilities intake needs and, for each, name the property it leans on, the risk, and the compensating design. Why: this is where "Claude can do it" turns into "Claude can do it if...". Done when: every capability has a row, and anything that must be exactly right comes from a system rather than the model. 3. Write the boundary conditions. List the conditions the design depends on, including the regulatory ones. Done when: each condition is specific enough that someone could tell whether it has been broken. 4. Give the verdict. Feasible as scoped, feasible with constraints, or not feasible, with one paragraph of reasoning and a rough monthly run cost at Tier M. Try it on your own work: pick one manual process you know and fill in the same four sections. 1. Baseline - Handling: 18,000 claims × 22 min = 6,600 handler hours a month , about $316,800 at $48 an hour. - Errors: 6% × 18,000 = 1,080 claims × 35 min rework = 630 hours , about $30,240 a month . - SLA: 81% acknowledged within one business day against a 98% target. 2. Capabilities against the four properties Capability Property Risk Design Read emails, forms and scans; extract the 31 fields Next-token prediction Plausible but wrong values (policy numbers, dates, amounts) Structured output against the schema; validate key fields against Policy Admin; low-confidence extractions to a handler Confirm the policy was active on the date of loss Training knowledge The model cannot know a policy's status Policy Admin API call; Claude never decides this Handle long medical reports Working memory 120-page packages are near the edge and costly 95% are under 20 pages; split or route the long tail to a handler Request missing documents, draft the acknowledgement Steerability Tone and content drift Template with fixed sections; structured fields filled from the extraction Decide cover or deny a claim (not a model task) Regulator forbids automated denials Stays with licensed adjusters; out of scope 3. Boundary conditions - Key fields (policy number, date of loss, claim amount) are validated against Policy Admin before a claim is created. - Extractions below the agreed confidence threshold go to a handler; the threshold is set from an evaluation, not guessed. - Packages over 20 pages follow a separate path (chunked processing or a handler). - No claim is denied or paid by the system; adjusters decide, and payouts over $10,000 need a senior adjuster. - EU claimants' data is processed through an EU route; US data stays in the US. 4. Verdict: feasible with constraints. Extraction, completeness checks and the acknowledgement draft play to Claude's strengths; the policy check and every decision stay with systems and people. The conditions above are part of the design. Run cost at Tier M is roughly 18,000 × 9,000 input tokens at $3 per million ( $486 ), the cached 4,000-token prefix at $0.30 per million ( about $22 ), and 1,200 output tokens at $15 per million ( $324 ): about $830 a month , small against a $316,800 baseline. Cost is not the constraint; accuracy on key fields and the regulatory boundary are. - My baseline is in hours and dollars, with the arithmetic shown. - Policy status comes from Policy Admin, not from the model. - Claim decisions stay with adjusters, and I said why. - My verdict is "feasible with constraints" and lists the constraints.

Design end-to-end architectures (input → processing → output → feedback loops). Design the whole path from input to output and back again, choose a reference architecture that fits the workload, and build in the reliability and feedback a demo never needs.

An end-to-end architecture covers four stages: input (what arrives and in what shape), processing (what Claude, your code and other systems do with it), output (what leaves the system, and in what form), and the feedback loop (how production results change the system over time). Exam scenarios often describe a design that handles the middle two well and forgets the first or the last.

A handful of shapes cover most enterprise workloads. Treat them as patterns to adapt and combine, not blueprints to copy. Shape Fits Built well Typical failure Agent Open-ended investigation where the steps cannot be listed in advance Narrow tool set, turn and token budgets, a clear stopping rule Unlimited autonomy and state-changing tools with no review Retrieval (RAG) Answering from a stable body of knowledge: manuals, policies, regulations Documents chunked and indexed; relevant chunks passed in as context Used for data that changes, such as order status or stock levels Document pipeline Pulling structured fields from claims, invoices or contracts OCR, extraction against a schema, validation, an exception route Low-confidence results flow on as if they were correct Routing Mixed incoming requests that need different handling Classify, then send each kind to retrieval, a transactional API or a person No path to a human; retrieval used for live data Coding agent Changing an unfamiliar codebase Agentic exploration, then fixed steps to plan, edit, test and review Edits merged without a human review gate Real systems mix these. A support assistant is often a router whose branches are a RAG lookup, an order-status API call and a human queue.

docs.h: Retrieval is for knowledge, tools are for live state
docs.c: Two kinds of data, two mechanisms
docs.x: The most common architectural mistake in this domain is answering a live-state question from an index. An index is a snapshot. If a customer asks where their order is, retrieval returns text about the order as it was when the index was last refreshed, and the answer sounds just as confident when it is wrong. No better embedding model or faster refresh cycle fixes this. The fix is to call the system that owns the data. Facts that stay true between index refreshes (policies, manuals, FAQs) belong in retrieval. Values owned by a system and changing on their own (balances, order status, availability) are fetched with a tool call at request time.

docs.h: A demo is not a production system
docs.x: A proof of concept hides four problems that production exposes: - Cost. Fifty requests a day cost almost nothing. The production bill must be modeled at real volume before the design is approved. - Latency. A single request in a demo says little about the 95th-percentile latency under concurrent load. - Reliability. A demo has no retries or fallbacks; the developer simply runs it again. Production needs them from the start. - Unexpected inputs. Demos are tested on inputs the builder expected. Production brings the ones nobody expected. Three reliability controls belong around every model call: retries with exponential backoff for transient errors such as rate limits and timeouts, a fallback (another model tier, a cached answer or a graceful message) when the primary path is unavailable, and a circuit breaker that stops calling a failing dependency so one outage does not cascade. They are far harder to add after launch than to design in.

docs.c: Claims intake, end to end · Fixing a stale-answer problem with better retrieval · An architecture with no way back
docs.x: The output stage is not the end. A complete architecture says how results are captured and acted on: 1. Signals. Logs, user ratings, escalations, corrections made by reviewers, eval scores. 2. Triage. Sort each signal: a defect, a gap in scope, a data problem or noise. 3. Decide. Agree who owns the fix and how urgent it is. 4. Act. Change the prompt, the data, the routing or the scope. 5. Review. Check the change worked, and add the failing case to the evaluation set so it cannot quietly return. Input: emailed claim forms and photos. Processing: extraction against a claim schema, a policy lookup through the insurer's API, a coverage check in the rules engine. Output: a structured claim record, plus a draft acknowledgement for the customer. Feedback: adjusters' corrections are logged against each field, low-confidence extractions go to a review queue, and every corrected case becomes a test case for the next prompt change. When a scenario shows answers that contradict the database or change after each re-index, options that tune chunking, embeddings or refresh frequency are distractors. The problem is the access pattern, not retrieval quality. A design that produces outputs but never captures corrections, ratings or failures cannot improve and cannot prove it works. Prefer options that feed production evidence back into evaluation.

Look for which stage the scenario is really about. If the symptom is wrong or stale facts, check the data access pattern. If the symptom is outages or cost overruns after launch, look for missing reliability controls or a cost model built from demo traffic. If the system "works" but nobody can show it is improving, the missing piece is the feedback loop. The best answer usually fixes the stage that failed rather than adding complexity elsewhere.

List each channel and what has to happen before Claude sees the content. Done when: all three channels from the case arrive in one consistent form. 2. Processing and outputs. List the stages in order. For each, name the owner (Claude, a system or a person) and what it produces. Why: naming the owner of every stage exposes steps that were silently given to the model. Done when: the final outputs are a created claim in ClaimsCore and a sent acknowledgement. 3. Reliability. Name three controls around the model calls, and what happens to a claim while Claude's API is unavailable. 4. Feedback loop. Describe how corrections made by handlers flow back into the system. Done when: a correction made today could stop the same error next month. Inputs Channel Before Claude Email Strip signatures and threads; save attachments to the document store Web form Structured fields kept as they are; photos stored Scanned mail OCR, with page images kept for reviewers All three become one "claim package": text, structured fields if any, links to attachments, channel, and received time. Processing and outputs Stage Owner Produces Extract the 31 fields Claude (structured output against the schema) Fields with a confidence per field Validate key fields, check policy status Policy Admin API plus rule checks Pass, mismatch or missing Fraud score Fraud rules engine Score and flags Route Code: rules on confidence, validation and size Straight-through, or handler queue with the reason Handler review (when routed) Intake handler Corrected fields Create the claim ClaimsCore API Claim record Draft and send the acknowledgement Claude drafts from a template; code sends Acknowledgement, plus any missing-document request Reliability - Retries with exponential backoff on rate limits, timeouts and server errors, with a cap on total wait. - A fallback: if the model is unavailable, packages wait in a durable queue and, past a set age, go to handlers so the one-day SLA still holds. - A circuit breaker on the extraction service so a failing dependency stops being called and the queue drains to people instead. Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM). Choose between an augmented LLM call, a workflow and an agent by asking which constraint is tightest, and default to the simplest pattern that meets it.
There are three ways to structure Claude's part in a system. The difference between them is who controls the sequence of steps : your code or the model.

One bounded call. You send a request, possibly with retrieval results, tools or extended thinking enabled, and Claude completes one job. Your application decides what happens next; nothing branches on the model's choices. Use it when the task is well defined and the result can be checked. Example: summarize a customer complaint and draft a reply for an agent to review.

The task is split into named steps that your code runs in a fixed order. Some steps call Claude, others call existing systems or apply rules. Because the control flow lives in code, each step can be logged, tested, monitored and audited like any other software. Use it when the steps are known in advance and mistakes are expensive. Workflows come in four common shapes: Shape How it works Example Chaining Each step consumes the previous step's output Extract obligations from a contract, then rate their risk, then write a summary Routing A classifier picks the path for each input Billing questions to account data, technical ones to product docs, complaints to a person Parallelization Independent pieces run at the same time and are combined Twelve supplier contracts reviewed concurrently, results merged into one report Evaluator-optimizer One call drafts, another checks against criteria, and the draft is revised until it passes or a retry limit is hit A customer reply checked against a tone and completeness rubric These shapes combine freely. A routed workflow can have a chained branch and an evaluator loop inside it.

Claude receives a goal and a set of tools and decides for itself which tools to call and in what order. The path is not written down anywhere you can inspect in advance. Use it only when the steps genuinely cannot be listed beforehand, such as investigating an unfamiliar codebase or researching across many sources, and when an unexpected result can be caught and recovered. A production agent always comes with limits: a minimal tool set, per-turn and total budgets, explicit permissions, a stopping condition, and human approval before consequential actions. These are part of the pattern, not optional extras.

docs.c: Start simple, escalate on evidence · Supplier onboarding checks · "The agent can handle anything" · Confusing tools with autonomy
docs.x: Walk through five factors. The first one that rules a pattern out usually decides. Factor Question Augmented LLM Workflow Agent Predictability Can the steps be listed in advance? One bounded task Yes, you wrote them No, by design Error cost What does a wrong answer cost? No guards between steps Checks between every step Errors can compound over many turns Observability Can operations reconstruct what happened? One call, easy to log Logs like ordinary code A long transcript that most tooling cannot alert on Latency What is the user-visible deadline? Fastest Predictable, adds up per step Open-ended; plan for the worst case Cost What is the cost per request at volume? Lowest Grows with steps Highest and least predictable Choose the simplest pattern that meets the requirements, then measure it in production. Move to a more autonomous pattern only when data shows the simpler one falling short. A manufacturer screens every new supplier through the same nine checks (sanctions list, tax registration, insurance certificate, and so on), and compliance must be able to show which check passed or failed for each supplier. The steps are known, errors are costly and every step must be reconstructable, so a workflow wins: code runs the checks in order, Claude reads the submitted certificates where interpretation is needed, and rule-based validation sits between steps. An agent choosing its own order would undermine the audit trail however capable it is. An agent is the most flexible pattern and also the least predictable, hardest to observe and most expensive. When a scenario lists fixed steps, audit needs or tight latency, the agent option is almost always the distractor. An augmented LLM call can use tools and retrieval and still not be an agent. What makes an agent is that the model decides the sequence across multiple steps, not that a tool is present.

Read the scenario for the deciding constraint. Phrases like "the steps never change", "every decision must be auditable" or "a three-second response" point to a workflow or a single call. Phrases like "the investigation path differs every time" or "unfamiliar codebase" point to an agent, and then the best option is the one that also bounds it with budgets, permissions and approval gates. When two options use the same pattern, prefer the one that adds the controls the scenario's risks call for.

docs.h: Apply it: Choose the pattern for support
docs.x: Hollis & Grant Home wants Claude in its chat and email support. One engineer proposes "a single agent with access to every system". Use the five factors to choose the pattern, then decide how each contact type is handled. 1. Score the five factors (predictability, error cost, observability, latency, cost) for Hollis & Grant's support, using the case facts. Done when: each factor has one line that quotes a fact from the case. 2. Name the deciding factor and the overall pattern it points to. Why: the exam rewards the simplest pattern that meets the tightest constraint. 3. Decide the handling for each contact type in the table from the case. Done when: every contact type has a path, and no state-changing action happens without the right check. 4. Say what evidence would justify an agent later, if any. 1. Five factors Factor Hollis & Grant Predictability Five known contact types cover all volume; the steps for each are known Error cost Wrong order status or a wrong refund is costly; refunds over $250 need a supervisor Observability Support leads must be able to see why a contact was answered as it was Latency Chat needs a first response within 3 seconds at the 95th percentile Cost $18,000 a month must cover peak season at 2.5 times normal volume 2. Deciding factor and pattern. Latency and predictability together rule out an open-ended agent: a multi-turn tool loop cannot reliably answer within 3 seconds, and the paths are known in advance. Handling per contact type Contact type Path Order status Augmented call: tool call to the Order Management System, then Claude phrases the answer Returns and refunds Workflow: Claude collects the details, the returns portal applies the rules, refunds over $250 go to a supervisor Product questions Retrieval over manuals and help centre, answer with a citation Account and billing Retrieval for policy questions; anything touching payment goes to an agent, and card data never enters the context Complaints Hand off to a person with a summary of the conversation 4. Evidence for an agent. Only if production data shows a meaningful share of contacts that the router cannot place and that need several look-ups in an unpredictable order, and only for email, where the 4-hour target leaves room for it. - I quoted the 3-second target and used it. - Order status comes from a tool call, not retrieval. - Refunds go through the returns portal's rules and the $250 approval. - I rejected the single agent with a reason, not a preference.

Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies. Know when an orchestrator with subagents is worth its cost, and design the decomposition, result format, conflict handling and failure recovery deliberately.

A multi-agent system splits work between two roles. - The orchestrator owns the goal. It breaks the work into sub-tasks, decides what to delegate, and combines the results into one answer. It coordinates rather than doing the sub-task work itself. - Subagents own scoped sub-tasks. Each runs in its own context window, completes one piece, and returns a result to the orchestrator.

docs.c: Multi-agent for breadth, not for sequence
docs.x: Multiple agents help when the work is broad and separable : many sources to research, many documents to review, many independent directions to explore. Each subagent gets a clean context focused on its piece, so the work is not squeezed into one crowded window, and independent pieces can run in parallel. They cost more. Every subagent carries its own instructions and context, so token use rises sharply compared with a single agent, and coordination adds latency and new failure points. Anthropic's write-up of its research system reports that multi-agent runs used many times the tokens of a chat interaction. That trade is worth making for high-value, parallel work and wasteful for tightly coupled tasks where every step depends on the last. If the sub-tasks are independent, parallel subagents can pay off. If each step needs the previous step's full result, a single agent or a chained workflow is cheaper and easier to debug.

docs.h: Three things you must design, not assume
docs.x: 1. Decomposition. How the goal is split, and how much each subagent is told. Vague task descriptions lead to duplicated work or gaps; each subagent needs a clear objective, boundaries and an expected output. 2. Result structure. Subagents should return results in a consistent, structured format, so the orchestrator can combine them without guessing. 3. Conflict resolution. When two subagents disagree or leave a gap, the orchestrator needs an explicit rule (prefer the more authoritative source, flag the conflict, or escalate to a person) rather than silently picking one.

docs.c: Supplier contract due diligence · Multi-agent as the default "advanced" answer · Treating every failure the same
docs.x: Where a failure happens decides whether it can be recovered. Failure Where it lands Design response A subagent returns nothing or malformed output The subagent boundary: recoverable Validate every result; retry or reassign the unit; record the gap instead of failing the whole run Subagents return conflicting results The synthesis step: recoverable Apply a stated conflict rule or escalate The orchestrator loses its goal or its partial synthesis The orchestrator: often unrecoverable Checkpoint its state so a run can resume rather than restart Traces scatter across agents Observability: affects everything Pass one trace ID through every agent so a run can be reconstructed Two practical consequences follow. Make subagent work idempotent , so a retry cannot double-apply an effect. And reconcile coverage at synthesis: the number of results should equal the number of units sent out, so a silently dropped subagent is noticed. An acquirer must review 100 supplier contracts before closing. The orchestrator splits them into one task per contract and sends them to subagents in parallel. Each subagent returns the same structured fields: change-of-control clauses, termination rights, liability caps, a risk rating. The orchestrator checks it has 100 results, retries any that failed validation, flags contracts where the risk rating conflicts with the clauses found, and writes the summary report from checkpointed partial results. Options that add an orchestrator and specialist agents to a simple, sequential task are distractors. More agents mean more cost, latency and failure points. A scenario that loses the orchestrator's state is a different problem from a single failed subagent. Retrying subagents does not help when the coordinator's progress is gone; checkpointing does.

Questions in this area usually present a working multi-agent design with one weakness: missing trace IDs, no conflict rule, no validation of subagent output, no checkpoint, or no check that every unit came back. Pick the option that fixes the stated weakness at the right boundary. If the scenario asks whether to use multiple agents at all, weigh independence of the sub-tasks against the extra token cost.

docs.h: Apply it: Plan the migration audit
docs.x: Northgate's platform team must audit all 160 services for the deprecated logging library within two weeks. By hand that is about 400 engineer-hours. Design a multi-agent audit that a platform engineer could run and trust. 1. Decide whether multi-agent fits. Use the independence of the work units to justify it, and name what the orchestrator does and does not do. 2. Define the subagent's task and its result format. List the fields every subagent must return. Why: the orchestrator can only combine results that share one structure. Done when: a "not sure" answer is possible and carries evidence. 3. Build the failure matrix. For at least four failures, say where each lands and the design response. 4. Make coverage provable. Say how the final report shows that all 160 services were audited, and what happens to the ones that were not. 1. Fit. Each service can be audited without knowing anything about the others, so the work is broad and separable: a good fit for parallel subagents with clean, focused contexts. The orchestrator reads the service catalogue, sends one task per service, validates and combines results, and writes the report. It does not audit code itself. 2. Task and result format. Task: "Audit service X in repository Y for use of the old logging library. Read only; change nothing." Each subagent returns: Field Values service, repository, owning team From the catalogue uses_old_library yes / no / unclear call_sites Number found patterns e.g. direct calls, wrapper class, configuration only risk low / medium / high, with a one-line reason evidence File paths and line numbers confidence high / medium / low 3. Failure matrix Failure Where it lands Response Subagent returns empty or malformed output Subagent boundary Validate against the format; retry once; then mark "needs human audit" Repository too large for one context Subagent Split by module; one subagent per module, merged per service Two runs disagree on a service Synthesis Rule: "yes" with evidence beats "no"; otherwise flag for the owning team Orchestrator crashes mid-run Orchestrator Results written to storage as they arrive; the run resumes from the checkpoint Results cannot be traced to a run Observability One run ID and the subagent's task ID on every result 4. Coverage. The report opens with a reconciliation line: 160 services in the catalogue, results received for N, validated M, and the list of services marked "needs human audit". Nothing is reported as complete until the counts match. The access is read-only throughout, which keeps the audit within Northgate's production-access rules. - My justification rests on independent units, not on "more agents are better". - The result format includes evidence and an "unclear" option. - My matrix separates subagent failures from orchestrator failures. - The report proves coverage with counts.

Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving. Break a complex process into pieces owned by Claude, by existing systems and by people, then split Claude's share along the lines that make it testable.

Decomposition is the step between "here is the business process" and "here is the architecture". Done well, it makes every later decision easier: each piece can be given to the right owner, tested on its own and replaced without disturbing the rest.

docs.h: First cut: who owns each piece
docs.c: Warranty claim handling
docs.x: Every solution has three possible owners. Owner What it should own Examples Claude Language work: reading, extracting, classifying, summarizing, planning, drafting Read a free-text complaint and identify the product and issue Existing systems Deterministic logic and authoritative data the business already trusts Account balances, eligibility rules, pricing, the record of truth People Judgment, exceptions, approvals, decisions where being right matters more than being fast Approving a large refund, deciding an unusual claim The most frequent mistake is to give everything to Claude because it can attempt everything. Over-assigning makes the system more expensive, slower, harder to audit and less accurate on precisely the tasks existing systems already do well. - Read the customer's description and photos and identify the fault: Claude . - Check whether the product is still under warranty: the warranty system . - Calculate the refund or replacement value: the pricing service , not the model. - Draft the customer response: Claude . - Approve claims above a value threshold or outside policy: a person .

docs.h: Second cut: how to split Claude's share
docs.x: Once you know what Claude owns, split that work along natural seams. Each seam maps to a workflow shape from lesson 1.3. - By stage : when one result feeds the next (extract, then classify, then summarize). This becomes a chain, and you can test each stage separately. - By input type : when different kinds of request need different handling. This becomes a router. - By independent unit : when the same task applies to many separate items, such as one per document or one per region. This becomes parallel work or subagents. - By draft and check : when quality can be verified but one attempt is not reliable enough. This becomes an evaluator-optimizer loop.

docs.h: Check each piece against the model's limits
docs.c: Numbers belong to code
docs.x: For every piece Claude owns, ask the four feasibility questions from lesson 1.1: - Does it need precise values ? Then the value comes from a system or from code, and Claude only works with it. - Does it need current or specialized knowledge ? Then bring that knowledge in through retrieval or a tool. - Does the input fit in the context window ? If not, split it further or load it progressively. - Is the instruction concrete and checkable ? If not, sharpen it, or move the logic into code. Totals, interest, tax, dosage, dates between events: anything that must be exactly right is computed deterministically, by an existing system or by code execution. Claude can explain the result; it should not be the calculator.

docs.h: Put people where the stakes are
docs.c: "Let Claude check the rules" · Decomposing too finely
docs.x: Human steps are part of the decomposition, not a patch added at the end. Place approval at the point where a decision becomes consequential or irreversible, such as issuing money, changing a record of truth, or sending something on the company's behalf. Routine, low-risk outputs can flow without review, which keeps reviewers focused on what matters. When a scenario includes a published policy, a rules table or an eligibility service, options that ask Claude to apply those rules from memory or from the prompt are usually distractors. The existing system applies the rule; Claude handles the language around it. Splitting work into many tiny model calls adds latency, cost and handoff errors. Split where there is a real seam: a different owner, a different input type, an independent unit, or a step you need to test on its own.

Decomposition questions usually describe a business process and ask which division of responsibilities is best. The right option gives language tasks to Claude, authoritative data and rules to existing systems, and consequential approvals to people, often with low-confidence cases routed to review. Watch for options that send authoritative checks to the model, remove a required human approval for speed, or make a person retype work that Claude could safely prepare.

Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs). Tie a design to the value the business actually cares about, express it in the business's own units, and build the cost and SLA case on measured numbers rather than averages and hopes.

A technically sound design still fails if nobody can show it is worth paying for. The exam expects you to connect architecture choices to named business outcomes and to defend them with numbers the business recognizes.

Most cases rest on one or two of these: Pillar The business question Typical measure Efficiency Do we do the same work with less effort? Handling time per case, cases per analyst per day Productivity Can our people do more, or more valuable, work? Output per person, time freed for higher-value tasks Transformation Can we do something we could not do before? New service, new channel, coverage that was not possible manually Cost Does it cost less to run than the alternative? Cost per transaction, total run cost against today's cost Performance and SLAs Does it meet the service level we promise? 95th-percentile response time, availability, accuracy threshold Name the pillar the stakeholder cares about first. A contact-centre director may care most about handling time; a compliance head may care about consistency and audit evidence; a product owner may want a new capability.

docs.h: Build the value case in four steps
docs.c: Three ways value cases go wrong
docs.x: 1. State today's baseline in a business unit. "Analysts spend 40 minutes per claim", measured from real operational data. 2. Predict the future state in the same unit. "15 minutes per claim, including review of the draft." 3. Subtract the run cost , taken from the sizing model rather than from a demo. 4. State the payback period and how sensitive it is to volume, adoption and accuracy. - An estimated baseline. If the "before" number was guessed, the claimed gain collapses the moment finance asks where it came from. - Assuming full automation when the design keeps a person in the loop. If reviewers check every output, labour is reduced, not eliminated, and the case must say so. - Costing from the average request. When a few very large requests drive most of the spend, an average understates run cost and overstates the return.

docs.c: SLAs are about the tail · Choosing the lever that does the work
docs.x: The sizing model takes call volume (from the business owner), tokens per request as a distribution, the model tier, and sensitivity scenarios. Then look at the levers: - Prompt caching cuts cost and latency when a long, stable prefix (system prompt, reference documents) repeats across many requests. Cache writes cost more than normal input, and cached content expires after a short time without use, so infrequent traffic gains little. - Batch processing lowers the price substantially for work that can wait, such as overnight document runs. It does not fit interactive, real-time use. For regulated data, confirm the batch route is covered by the same compliance arrangements. - A smaller model tier for simpler steps, with an evaluation proving quality holds. - Output length limits where long answers add cost without adding value. Promise and measure the 95th or 99th percentile, under realistic concurrent load, not the median from a single test request. A design that is fast on average can still breach its SLA every afternoon. An HR policy assistant answers 80,000 employee questions a month. Every request carries the same 7,000-token block of policy text and instructions, and the projected bill is well over budget. Switching to the largest model makes it worse; raising the output limit does nothing for cost. Caching that repeated block removes most of the repeated input cost and also reduces latency, which is why it is the first lever to pull here.

Value questions usually give you a stakeholder, a goal and some numbers. The best answer states the benefit in the stakeholder's unit, builds on a measured baseline, includes the real run cost and the human review the design requires, and chooses the cost or latency lever that matches the workload's shape. Be wary of options that promise savings from full automation, quote average latency for an SLA, or pick the most capable model without a reason tied to the stated pillar.

Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs. Pick the model tier that meets the quality bar inside the cost and latency budgets, route by task difficulty where it pays, and treat every model change as a release that needs an evaluation.
The architect's job is not to pick the most powerful model. It is to pick the model that meets the application's quality requirement within its cost and latency budgets, and to prove it.

Claude models come in tiers that trade capability against speed and price. Tier Strength Typical work Smallest and fastest (Haiku family) Lowest latency and cost per token Classification, routing, simple extraction, high-volume short tasks Balanced (Sonnet family) Strong reasoning at moderate cost Most enterprise work: drafting, analysis, coding, tool use Most capable (Opus family) Deepest reasoning on hard problems Complex analysis, difficult multi-step agents, tasks where the balanced tier measurably falls short These are starting points, not rules. The right answer for a workload is the one the evaluation supports.

docs.c: Start in the middle, move on evidence
docs.x: 1. How hard is the reasoning? Sorting tickets into five categories is not the same as weighing contract clauses against each other. 2. How costly is a mistake? Nuanced judgment may justify a stronger model. Factual or numerical precision usually does not: no tier replaces an authoritative data source or a calculation in code. 3. What is the latency budget? A user waiting in a chat window has a hard ceiling; an overnight batch does not. 4. What does it cost at volume? A small difference per request becomes large at hundreds of thousands of requests a month. Begin with the balanced tier for most work. Move up only when an evaluation shows the quality gap; move down when an evaluation shows the smaller tier still meets the bar with better cost or latency.

When a workload mixes easy and hard requests, one model for everything wastes money on the easy ones or quality on the hard ones. A model-routing design classifies each request first (usually with a small, fast model) and sends it to the tier that suits it. Routing only works when the classifier is reliable and the difference in difficulty is real; otherwise it adds a failure point for no gain.

Extended thinking lets a model reason before answering, with an effort level or token budget you control. It can raise quality on multi-step problems without changing tier, but it adds latency and output tokens. If latency is the tightest constraint, turning thinking up may break the budget; if quality is the gap, more thinking on the balanced tier may be cheaper than moving to the top tier.

docs.h: A model change is a release
docs.c: Cutting cost without guessing · "Use the most capable model to be safe" · Fixing wrong facts with a bigger model
docs.x: Swapping models is a one-line code change and a whole-application behaviour change. Prompts tuned for one model can behave differently on another, even a newer one. Before any switch you need: - a curated test set of representative inputs with known-good outcomes, - a grading method (code checks, a rubric scored by a model, or human review), - an acceptance threshold agreed before the run, plus a rollback plan. Keep a regression suite for behaviour that already works, so an upgrade that improves one area cannot silently break another. An insurer wants to move claim triage from the balanced tier to the small tier to save money. The architect runs 500 labelled historical claims through both, scores them with the same grader, and compares against the threshold agreed with operations (no more than a 1-point drop in routing accuracy, and no drop at all on fraud-flagged claims). The small tier passes on routine claims and fails on fraud-flagged ones, so the final design routes fraud-flagged claims to the balanced tier and the rest to the small one. Choosing the top tier by default is a classic distractor. It costs the most, is often slower, and is not evidence-based. The right option names the requirement and the evaluation. If answers contain wrong prices, balances or dates, a stronger model is not the fix. The values must come from the system that owns them.

Model questions usually give a workload, a volume, a latency target and a quality concern, then ask what to choose or what to do before switching. Look for answers that tie the tier to a stated constraint, route mixed workloads by difficulty, and gate any change on an evaluation with a threshold set in advance. Distractors switch models straight away to save money, assume a newer model needs no testing, or reach for the largest model without a reason.

Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails. Write system prompts with a clear role, explicit constraints and an output contract, build them as templates whose fixed rules cannot be overwritten, and enforce anything consequential outside the prompt.

A production system prompt is a specification, not a greeting. "You are a helpful support assistant" leaves almost every decision to chance. The exam expects prompts that make behaviour predictable and controls that do not depend on the prompt alone.

docs.h: Three parts of every production system prompt
docs.x: Part Answers Example content Role and scope Who is Claude here, and what is in and out of scope? "You answer questions about Hollis & Grant products and orders. You do not give legal or financial advice." Constraints What must always or never happen, and what to do when information is missing? "Never state a delivery date that the order system did not return. If the manual does not cover the question, say so and offer an agent." Output contract What shape does the answer take? Fields, length limits, citation format, an escalation flag Explaining why a rule exists helps the model apply it sensibly to cases the rule did not foresee. "Do not quote prices, because prices change daily and only the catalogue is current" generalizes better than "do not quote prices".

docs.c: Contracts belong in structure, not hope
docs.x: A reusable prompt is a template : fixed instructions plus slots filled per request. Fixed scaffolding Variable slots Role, scope, tone The customer's message Safety and business rules Retrieved manual passages Escalation rules Customer and order details from systems Output format The conversation so far Two design rules keep templates safe: - Mark the slots clearly , for example with XML-style tags such as <customer_message> and <manual_excerpt> , and tell the model that content inside them is data to work with, not instructions to follow. - Never put a mandatory rule inside a slot that a user, a document or another system can fill. A rule that lives in a user-controlled field can be removed or contradicted by that user. If downstream code parses the answer, use structured outputs (a JSON schema the response must match) rather than "please answer in JSON". The schema is enforced; the request is only followed most of the time.

A prompt guides behaviour; it does not enforce it. For anything consequential, the rule also lives outside the model. Layer Example for refunds Prompt instruction "Do not promise refunds the policy does not allow" Application check The returns service rejects ineligible refunds whatever Claude says Permission The assistant's credentials cannot call the refund endpoint above $250 Human approval A supervisor approves refunds over $250 The prompt reduces how often the model tries the wrong thing. The other layers make sure that when it does, nothing bad happens.

docs.c: A support prompt that holds up · The safety rule in the wrong place · Prompt-only enforcement
docs.x: System prompts belong in version control with an owner, a change history and the evaluation that approved each version. A prompt edit can change behaviour as much as a model change, so it goes through the same test gate. Role: answers product and order questions for Hollis & Grant customers. Constraints: order facts come only from the order tool result; product facts only from the cited manual excerpt; anything about payment cards goes to an agent; if unsure, say so. Output contract: answer, citation, escalate true or false with a reason. Slots: <order_data> , <manual_excerpt> , <conversation> . Enforcement outside the prompt: refunds go through the returns service, and card data is stripped before it reaches the model. A design that puts "never reveal other customers' data" into a field the customer's own message can influence is unsafe, however well it is worded. Fixed rules live in the fixed scaffolding. Options that rely on a stronger instruction ("NEVER issue refunds over $250") to stop a consequential action are distractors when an application check, a permission or an approval step is available.

Expect a weak prompt or a failing assistant and four improvements. Strong answers add the missing part (scope, constraint or output contract), separate fixed instructions from untrusted input, use structured outputs for machine-read responses, and back consequential rules with checks outside the model. Watch for options that only reword or capitalize an instruction, or that move rules into user-controlled content.

Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought). Know when zero-shot is enough, when examples teach better than instructions, and when to ask for step-by-step reasoning, and add each technique only when an evaluation shows the need.
The exam guide names three techniques: zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought. The skill being tested is choosing between them for a given task, and knowing what each one cannot do.

You describe the task, the inputs and the expected output, and give no worked examples. It is the right starting point for well-defined tasks: classifying into clearly separated categories, summarizing to a stated length, extracting named fields. Most quality problems at this stage are fixed by being clearer and more specific, not by adding techniques.

docs.h: Few-shot: show, do not just tell
docs.x: You include a handful of input and output pairs. Examples work best when the desired behaviour is easier to show than to describe: a house style, a subtle boundary between categories, a judgment pattern. Good example sets are: - Representative of the real input mix, not only the easy cases. - Diverse , so the model learns the pattern rather than copying one surface feature. - Strong on boundaries , including the cases people also argue about. - Consistent , with no two examples that contradict each other. - Clearly marked , for example inside <example> tags, so they are not confused with the real input.

docs.c: A progression, not a menu
docs.x: For multi-step problems, asking the model to work through the problem before giving its answer, or enabling extended thinking, often improves quality. Structured prompts help: "first list the relevant policy clauses, then compare each to the claim, then give the recommendation." Separating the reasoning from the final answer (for example in different tags or fields) keeps the output clean for downstream code. Reasoning costs tokens and time, so use it where the task genuinely has several steps, not everywhere. Start zero-shot and measure. Add examples when consistency or judgment falls short. Add reasoning when the task has real intermediate steps. Re-measure after each change, and stop adding when the evaluation stops improving. Technique Examples? Best for Cost Zero-shot No Clear, well-specified tasks Lowest Few-shot Yes Formats, styles and boundaries that are easier to demonstrate More input tokens Chain-of-thought Not needed Multi-step analysis and judgment More output tokens and latency

Reasoning makes a calculation more likely to be right; it does not make it right. Exact arithmetic, dates and policy rules still belong in code or authoritative systems. Likewise, examples cannot supply facts the model does not have.

docs.h: Long documents need their own care
docs.x: When a prompt contains long documents, put the documents before the instructions and the question, wrap each one in tags with its source, and ask the model to quote the relevant passages before answering. Quote-first answers are easier to verify and less likely to drift from the source.

docs.c: Fixing a boundary problem with examples · Reasoning as a substitute for computation · Examples that only show easy cases
docs.x: The same prompt can behave differently on another model tier or generation. A capable model may need less scaffolding; a smaller one may need more examples. Re-evaluate prompts on the model that will actually run them. A ticket classifier confuses "billing dispute" with "refund request". Rewriting the instructions helps a little. Adding six examples, three of each, including two tickets that mention both money and a faulty product, fixes most of the errors because the boundary is now visible. When a scenario needs an exact figure (a premium, a pro-rated refund, a dosage), options that add chain-of-thought or extended thinking are distractors. The figure is computed in code or by the owning system. A few-shot set made of obvious cases teaches nothing about the hard boundary. Prefer the option that adds representative and borderline examples.

Technique questions describe a task and a symptom: inconsistent format, wrong category on borderline inputs, shallow analysis, or wrong numbers. Match the symptom to the technique. Inconsistency or subtle categories point to few-shot; shallow multi-step analysis points to reasoning; wrong numbers point to code or tools, not prompting. Answers that pile on every technique at once, or skip measurement, are usually wrong.

Optimize context windows and manage token usage. Decide what goes into the context window and when, using monolithic, progressive, retrieval and compaction strategies, and prevent the two different ways a request can run out of room.

Prompt engineering is about the instructions. Context engineering is about everything else the model sees: which documents, tool results and history are in the window, when they arrive, and how long they stay. It drives quality, cost and latency at the same time.

Every call carries the system prompt, tool definitions, the conversation so far, retrieved documents, tool results and the space needed for the answer (plus thinking, if enabled). Anything outside the window does not exist for that call. A bigger window is not automatically better. More tokens cost more and take longer, and long, cluttered context makes the relevant detail harder to find. The goal is the smallest set of high-signal tokens that lets the model do the step in front of it.

docs.h: Four things that are easy to confuse
docs.x: Concept What it is Who owns it Context window What the model can see on this call The request you build Retrieval Fetching relevant knowledge at the time of the question Your retrieval layer Application state The authoritative record: orders, cases, patients Your systems of record Memory and summaries Selected facts carried between calls or sessions Your application (or a memory tool you provide) The API does not remember previous calls. If a conversation, a decision or an identifier needs to persist, your application stores it and sends it again.

docs.c: Compaction must keep the facts that matter
docs.x: Strategy Idea Fits Main risk Monolithic Load everything needed up front Bounded tasks with predictable inputs that need all the material at once Cost and clutter as content grows Progressive Load only what the next step needs Multi-step workflows, agents, long conversations Dropping something an earlier step needed Retrieval Fetch relevant pieces at question time Large or changing knowledge, citations Retrieval misses the right passage Compaction Summarize accumulated history and continue Long-running agents and sessions near the limit Losing exact identifiers, numbers and decisions Real systems combine them. A coding agent might start with a full task description, add files progressively as it explores, retrieve documentation on demand, clear old tool results it no longer needs, and compact its history after many turns. A summary that loses an account number, a dosage or a decision is worse than no summary. Tell the compaction step exactly what to preserve verbatim, or keep those facts in structured application state instead.

docs.h: Two different ways to run out of room
docs.c: An agent that kept everything · "Use a bigger context window" · Expecting the API to remember
docs.x: 1. The request is too large to send. The prompt is over the model's token limit (rejected as an invalid request) or the request body is over the byte limit (rejected as too large). Nothing is generated. 2. The request fits, but the answer runs into the ceiling. Generation stops early with a stop reason saying the context window was exceeded, and the output is cut off. Prevention is mostly measurement: count tokens before sending large requests, read the usage figures on every response, reserve room for the output, and trim what does not earn its place (old tool results, repeated instructions, whole documents where a section would do). A research agent re-read 40 web pages per task and carried every page in its history. By the end, each call held over 150,000 tokens, costs had tripled and answers had become vaguer. Clearing tool results once they had been summarized into notes, and keeping those notes in structured state, cut the context by 80% and improved the answers. When a scenario shows rising cost, slower responses or degraded answers in long sessions, the larger-window option is usually the distractor. First stop sending what is not needed. Options that assume Claude recalls an earlier call, or that the conversation persists on its own, are wrong. The application carries state forward.

Context questions describe long documents, long sessions or growing agents, often with a symptom: the request is rejected, answers are cut off, answers get worse late in a session, or costs climb. Identify which of the two failure modes it is, pick the strategy that fits the data and the task, and look for compaction that preserves identifiers. Be suspicious of options that only enlarge the window or rely on the model's memory.

docs.t: Prompt Reuse: Caching, Modular Prompts and Skills
docs.x: Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills). Reuse prompts three ways: cache stable prefixes to cut cost and latency, share prompt fragments as a modular library, and package governed procedures as Skills, and know which one each situation needs.

docs.t: Prompt Reuse: Caching, Modular Prompts and Skills
docs.x: "Reuse" covers three different mechanisms that solve three different problems. Exam questions often hinge on telling them apart. Mechanism Reuses Solves Prompt caching Processing of an identical prompt prefix Cost and latency of sending the same long prefix again and again Modular prompt library Prompt fragments and templates Duplication and drift of instructions across a codebase Skills A complete, packaged procedure Consistent, governed execution of a task across teams

docs.t: Prompt Reuse: Caching, Modular Prompts and Skills
docs.c: Caching is not memory
docs.x: When many requests start with the same content (system prompt, tool definitions, reference documents, stable examples), caching lets later requests read that prefix from cache instead of processing it again. Cached reads cost a fraction of normal input and arrive faster. How to design for it: - Static first, dynamic last. Put everything that never changes at the start and the per-request content (user message, customer data) after it. A cache breakpoint marks where the reusable prefix ends. - Keep the prefix byte-for-byte identical. Any change before the breakpoint is a cache miss: a timestamp in the system prompt, reordered tool definitions, a changed example. - Match the lifetime to the traffic. Cached content expires if unused for a short time (minutes by default, with a longer option at a higher write cost). Steady traffic keeps it warm; a few requests a day do not. - Count the write cost. Writing to the cache costs more than normal input, so caching pays only when the prefix is long enough and read often enough. Caching reuses the processing of identical text. It does not store conversation history, remember a user, or retrieve new knowledge. Options that use caching for "remembering" are wrong. When hit rates are lower than expected, cache diagnostics report why a request missed: usually something before the breakpoint changed.

docs.t: Prompt Reuse: Caching, Modular Prompts and Skills
docs.x: A library of reusable prompt fragments (a code-review checklist, a tone guide, a citation rule) that engineers assemble into their own prompts. It is lightweight and flexible and suits a team or a codebase. Its weakness is drift: copies diverge, versions are hard to track, and different teams end up with different variants.

docs.t: Prompt Reuse: Caching, Modular Prompts and Skills
docs.c: A Skill is a procedure, not a long prompt · One fix, two mechanisms · The invisible cache breaker
docs.x: A Skill packages a whole procedure: instructions in a SKILL.md file, plus optional scripts and reference files. Claude sees a short description of each available Skill and loads the full contents only when a task needs it, so many Skills can be available without filling the context window. Skills can be versioned, reviewed and distributed, which makes them the choice when a procedure must run the same way everywhere. Need Choose A few shared phrases or checklists that teams adapt Prompt library A repeatable procedure that must be consistent across teams Skill Versioning, approval and rollback Skill The procedure needs scripts or reference files Skill Lower cost and latency for a repeated long prefix Caching (works with either) If the requirement mentions governance, versions, distribution across teams or bundled scripts, the answer is a Skill. If it mentions cost or latency of a repeated prefix, the answer is caching. A bank's twelve engineering teams each paste their own copy of a release checklist into prompts, and copies have drifted. The fix is a release Skill owned by the platform team, versioned and reviewed. Separately, the CI bot that runs the Skill sends the same 8,000-token instructions on every pull request; caching that prefix cuts its cost and latency. The Skill fixes consistency; caching fixes cost. A scenario with a low cache hit rate and a system prompt that "includes the current date and time at the top" is pointing at the cause. Move dynamic content after the breakpoint.

docs.t: Prompt Reuse: Caching, Modular Prompts and Skills
docs.x: Reuse questions describe either a cost or latency problem with repeated content, or a consistency and governance problem with shared instructions. Pick caching for the first and a Skill (or a library, if flexibility matters more than governance) for the second. For caching scenarios, check the prompt order and anything that changes per request before the breakpoint.

docs.h: Apply it: Untangle reuse at Northgate
docs.x: Northgate's teams each keep their own code-review prompt, and the security lead wants every review to apply the same secrets checklist. Meanwhile, the CI review bot sends a 9,000-token instruction block on each of about 300 pull requests per working day, its cache hit rate is 0%, and its system prompt starts with the pull request number. 1. Decide the mechanism for each need : the secrets checklist, each team's style preferences, and a release-notes procedure that runs a version-check script. 2. Fix the CI bot's caching and explain why the hit rate is zero. 3. Estimate the monthly saving on the instruction block at Tier M, assuming 22 working days and that the cache stays warm through the working day. Done when: you can say whether the saving alone justifies the work, or what else does. 1. Mechanisms Need Mechanism Why Secrets checklist in every review Skill, owned by security, versioned Must be identical everywhere and approved Team style preferences Team prompt fragments or each repository's project instructions Teams need to adapt them; governance is light Release notes with a version-check script Skill A procedure with a bundled script, used across teams 2. Caching. The pull request number at the top changes on every request, so the prefix is never identical and every call misses. Move it, and all other per-request data, after the stable instructions and set the breakpoint at the end of the instruction block. 3. Saving. 300 × 22 = 6,600 reviews a month. Uncached: 6,600 × 9,000 = 59.4 million tokens × $3 per million = about $178 . Cached reads at 10%: about $18 , plus a few cache writes a day. Saving: about $160 a month . On its own that does not justify much engineering time; the stronger reasons are lower latency on every review and the fact that the fix is a few lines. The Skill, not caching, solves the consistency problem. - The secrets checklist is a Skill, not a pasted fragment. - I explained the zero hit rate with the changing prefix. - My arithmetic uses the assumed Tier M price. - I did not claim caching fixes consistency.

Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent). Choose between the API, the SDKs, the Agent SDK, MCP, Claude Code and agent-to-agent designs by what Claude has to do and who uses it, and pick the delivery route the organization's constraints allow.

Integration choices sit at two levels: how your code talks to Claude (the build-time interface) and where the traffic goes (the delivery route). The exam tests both, and especially the cases where two options look interchangeable but are not.

Interface What it gives you Choose it when Trade-off Direct API Raw HTTP requests and responses You need full control, or a new feature is not in the SDK yet You build retries, streaming and tool plumbing yourself Client SDKs The same API with typed, language-native helpers The default for embedding Claude in a product Your code still owns any loop or orchestration Agent SDK A managed agent loop: iteration, tool execution, termination Claude must act over many turns inside your own application Less control over each individual turn MCP An open protocol for exposing tools, resources and prompts from a server The same tools must be reachable from several Claude clients An extra protocol layer to run and debug Claude Code An agentic coding tool for engineers The user is a developer working in a codebase Not a backend for a customer-facing product Two distinctions come up again and again: - MCP and the Agent SDK are different layers. MCP is how tools are exposed; the Agent SDK is the loop that decides when to call them. They are often used together. - MCP versus plain tool use. If the tools live inside one product, define them directly with tool use. MCP earns its extra layer when the same tools must serve several clients (Claude Code, Claude apps, an internal portal).

Sometimes one agent hands work to another: an orchestrator delegating to specialist subagents in the same system, or two separately owned agents exchanging tasks. Inside one system, treat it as the orchestration design from lesson 1.4, with structured results and shared trace IDs. Across organizational boundaries it is an integration contract: define the message format, authenticate both sides, limit what each agent may ask the other to do, and log every exchange.

docs.c: Constraints first, convenience second · Choosing for a hospital · "Use MCP for everything" · Claude Code as a product backend
docs.x: The same models are available directly from Anthropic and through major cloud platforms (for example Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI and Microsoft's catalogue). Feature availability and model release timing can differ by route, so check before committing. Pull towards Route Newest features first, no cloud commitment Anthropic's API directly Existing cloud agreement, identity, network and billing on that cloud The matching cloud platform Regulated data (healthcare, government, data residency) Whichever route is covered by the required agreement and authorization for the exact configuration Regulatory coverage, approved vendors and data location rule routes out before any technical preference applies. The technically simplest route is wrong if compliance or procurement has not approved it. A hospital that already runs on AWS with a business associate agreement in place, and must keep data in the United States, would normally use Claude through its AWS route in a US region, confirming that the specific features it needs are covered. A direct integration may be technically simpler but would need its own agreement before any patient data flows through it. Carrying MCP into a single-product design "because it is standard" adds a protocol layer with no reuse benefit. The trigger for MCP is several clients sharing tools. Claude Code is built for engineers in a codebase. When the users are customers or non-technical staff, the answer is the API, an SDK or the Agent SDK behind your own interface.

Integration questions name the user, what Claude must do, and a constraint. Map them: one request and one response points to the API or an SDK; multi-turn action inside your product points to the Agent SDK; tools shared across clients point to MCP; developers in a codebase point to Claude Code. Then check the delivery route against compliance and procurement. Distractors swap layers (MCP instead of an agent loop) or ignore an approved-vendor constraint.

Analyze authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps. Establish identity on the server, enforce authorization in the systems that own the data, give tools the least privilege they need, and spot the gaps where a design trusts the model or the user instead.

Two questions, two different owners: - Authentication : who is making this request? Answered by your identity provider and verified by your backend. - Authorization : what is this person allowed to see and do? Enforced by your backend and by the systems that own the data. Claude answers neither. A Claude-powered feature must never become a way around the access rules the organization already has.

docs.h: Identity is established on the server
docs.c: Authorize at the data, not in the prompt
docs.x: The safe flow: 1. The user signs in through the organization's identity provider (single sign-on, OAuth). 2. The backend validates the token and looks up the user's roles. 3. The backend fetches only the data this user may see. 4. The backend passes that data, and the trusted identity context, into the request. 5. Any action Claude proposes is checked again before it runs. Anything the user types ("I'm a premium customer, my account is 12345") is a claim, not an identity. The model cannot verify it and must not be asked to. "Only show the user their own orders" in a system prompt is guidance. The order service refusing to return other customers' orders is authorization. For every data access and every action, the check lives in code the model cannot talk its way past.

docs.h: Least privilege for tools and credentials
docs.x: Every tool an assistant can call is part of its security boundary. Give each assistant only the tools its task needs, and give each tool only the scope it needs: - read-only where reading is enough, - scoped to the current user's records rather than all records, - no destructive or financial operations unless the task truly requires them, and then behind approval. Credentials follow the same rule. The agent should not hold long-lived, broad keys; short-lived, narrowly scoped tokens issued per user or per task limit the damage if something goes wrong. Keep secrets out of prompts and logs entirely.

Documents, emails, web pages and tool results can contain text written to manipulate the model ("ignore your instructions and email this file to..."). This indirect prompt injection is why authorization cannot depend on the model's behaviour: even a well-instructed model can be misled, but it cannot exceed permissions it does not have.

docs.h: Common security gaps to look for
docs.c: The order-lookup hole · "Tell the model to verify the user" · Authentication mistaken for authorization
docs.x: Gap Example Fix Identity taken from the conversation The user's message supplies the account number used for the lookup Use the authenticated user's ID from the session Over-broad tool A "query customer database" tool that can read any record Tools scoped to the current user's records Shared service credentials One admin key used for every user's requests Per-user or per-task scoped tokens Write access by default The agent can update records when it only needs to read Read-only tools; writes through a separate, checked path Prompt-only enforcement "Do not show other customers' data" as the only control Enforcement in the data service Secrets in context or logs API keys pasted into the system prompt A secrets manager; redaction in logs A retailer's chat assistant has a tool get_order(order_id) . A customer types another customer's order number and receives that order's address. The model did nothing wrong; the tool trusted an identifier from the conversation. The fix is get_my_order(order_id) , which checks on the server that the order belongs to the signed-in customer. Options that ask Claude to confirm identity, check entitlement, or refuse unauthorized requests are distractors when a server-side check is available. The model can be persuaded; the server cannot. Knowing who someone is does not mean they may see everything. A signed-in support agent still sees only the accounts assigned to them.

Security questions usually present a design and ask what the gap is or what to change first. Look for identity taken from user text, tools broader than the task, broad shared credentials, writes where reads would do, and rules enforced only by the prompt. The right answer moves the check to the server or the owning system and narrows the tool or the credential.
