docs.x: A Hollis & Grant engineer proposes this design for the order and returns assistant: the chat widget sends the customer's message and the email address they type; the backend calls the Order Management System with a shared admin API key; the assistant has tools get_order(order_id) , create_return(order_id, items) and issue_refund(order_id, amount) ; the system prompt says "only discuss the customer's own orders and never refund more than $250". 1. List every security gap you can find, using the table in this lesson. 2. Redesign the identity and tool layer so each gap is closed in code. Done when: nothing depends on the customer's typed details or on the prompt for enforcement. 3. Say where approval still involves a person. 1. Gaps - Identity comes from a typed email address, not a signed-in session. - get_order(order_id) returns any order whose number the customer knows. - A shared admin key gives every request full access to the order system. - The assistant can issue refunds directly; the $250 limit is only a prompt instruction. - Nothing stops an injected instruction (for example in a pasted message) from triggering a refund. 2. Redesign - Customers must be signed in to discuss orders; the backend takes the customer ID from the session token. - Tools become get_my_orders() and get_my_order(order_id) , which check ownership on the server, and request_return(order_id, items) , which creates a return request through the returns portal's normal rules. - The backend calls the order system with a scoped, short-lived token for that customer, not an admin key. - issue_refund is removed from the assistant. Refunds are created by the returns portal after its own eligibility checks. 3. People. Refunds over $250 go to a supervisor in the returns portal, as today. The assistant can tell the customer that a request is with a supervisor; it cannot approve it. - Identity comes from the session, not the chat. - Tools are scoped to the signed-in customer. - The admin key is gone. - The refund limit is enforced by the returns portal, not the prompt.

Evaluate tool/agent configuration for capability bloat. Recognize when an agent has more tools, servers or permissions than its task needs, and cut it back to a small, well-described tool set that is cheaper, more accurate and safer.

Capability bloat is what happens when an agent accumulates tools, connected servers and permissions beyond what its job requires. It usually arrives gradually: someone connects a whole MCP server when one tool was needed, a "just in case" admin tool is left in, every team adds its favourite integration.

Cost What happens Accuracy With many similar tools, the model picks the wrong one or calls several where one would do Tokens and latency Every tool definition is sent on every call; dozens of tools can add thousands of tokens per request Security Every tool is something an injected instruction or a mistake can use Operations More integrations to monitor, version and debug

docs.c: Every tool must justify itself
docs.x: 1. Start from the task, not the catalogue. List the actions the job actually needs. Everything else goes. 2. Prefer a few purposeful tools over many thin ones. One get_customer_summary that returns the fields the task needs beats five low-level endpoints the model must chain together. 3. Give every tool a clear, distinct description : what it does, when to use it, what its parameters mean, and how it differs from similar tools. Overlapping descriptions cause wrong choices. 4. Return only what the task needs. Tool responses go into the context too. Return the relevant fields, paginate or summarize large results, and give helpful errors instead of stack traces. 5. Split by role. If two parts of a job need different tools, give them to different agents or subagents, each with its own small set, rather than one agent with the union. 6. Load on demand when the set is genuinely large. When an agent really does need access to hundreds of tools, a tool search capability lets it discover and load only the relevant ones (lesson 3.4). For each tool ask: which step of the task uses it, and what happens if it is removed? If nothing breaks, remove it. If it changes state, it also needs a reason to exist without approval.

docs.c: The support agent with 60 tools · "More tools make the agent more capable" · Solving bloat with a bigger model
docs.x: Bloat also hides in configuration: broad permission modes, write access to whole file systems, network access the task does not need, many MCP servers enabled globally instead of per project. The same discipline applies: the narrowest configuration that lets the task succeed. A support agent connected to the company's full CRM MCP server could see 60 tools, including bulk export and account deletion. It often called search_contacts when get_customer was right, and every request carried about 9,000 tokens of tool definitions. Cutting to six task-specific tools improved tool-choice accuracy in the evaluation, cut input tokens by about 8,000 per request, and removed deletion from the attack surface. Options that add tools or connect whole servers "for flexibility" are usually wrong when the scenario mentions wrong tool choices, rising cost, or a security concern. A larger model may cope slightly better with a cluttered tool list, but it costs more and leaves the security exposure. Trimming the tool set addresses the cause.

Look for symptoms: the agent calls the wrong tool, requests are expensive before the user has typed anything, or a tool exists that the task never needs (especially a destructive one). The best answer trims or consolidates tools, sharpens descriptions, splits roles, or loads tools on demand. Distractors add more instructions about tool choice, move to a bigger model, or keep dangerous tools behind a prompt warning.

Evaluate progressive discovery vs. monolithic context strategy. Decide whether an agent should get everything up front or discover tools, knowledge and instructions as it goes, and use Skills, tool search and just-in-time retrieval to keep a large capability set from flooding the context.

Lesson 2.4 compared context strategies for data . This task applies the same choice to an agent's capabilities : its tools, its procedures and the knowledge it may need. Should all of it be in the context from the first turn (monolithic), or should the agent find and load what it needs as it goes (progressive discovery)?

Monolithic Progressive discovery How Every tool definition, instruction and reference document is loaded up front The agent starts with a short index and loads details when the task calls for them Strength Simple, predictable, nothing to look up, easy to cache Scales to large capability sets; the context stays focused Weakness Cost and clutter grow with every capability added; selection accuracy drops An extra step to find things; the agent can fail to discover what it needs Fits Small, stable capability sets; short tasks that use most of what is loaded Large or growing tool and procedure libraries; long-running agents

docs.c: Monolithic until it hurts, then discover
docs.x: - Skills. Only each Skill's name and short description sit in the context. When a task matches, the agent reads the full instructions, and only then any scripts or reference files inside the Skill. Dozens of procedures stay available at almost no standing cost. - Tool search. Instead of sending hundreds of tool definitions, the agent gets a search capability and loads the few relevant tools for the current step. - Just-in-time retrieval. The agent holds lightweight references (file paths, document IDs, queries) and fetches content when it needs it, the way a person uses a file system rather than memorizing it. - Subagents. A subagent explores in its own context and returns a condensed result, so the main agent never carries the raw material. If the whole capability set is small and nearly always used, load it up front and cache it. When tools or procedures number in the dozens, change often, or are mostly unused on a given task, switch to progressive discovery.

docs.c: A developer environment that grew · Discovery for a tiny tool set · Everything in the always-loaded instructions
docs.x: Discovery fails silently when the agent cannot tell what exists. Descriptions and names carry the load: each Skill's description must say clearly when to use it; each tool's name and summary must be findable by the words a task would use. Test discovery itself in evaluations: given a task, did the agent find and load the right capability? An engineering team's Claude Code setup had 25 MCP servers enabled for everyone and a 30,000-token project instruction file covering every procedure. Sessions started slowly, cost more, and Claude sometimes followed the wrong procedure. The team cut the always-loaded instructions to the conventions every task needs, moved the procedures into Skills, enabled MCP servers per project instead of globally, and the starting context fell by more than 80%. Adding tool search or a retrieval layer for an agent with five tools adds a step and a failure mode for no benefit. Monolithic is correct when the set is small. Putting every procedure into the instructions loaded on every request is the monolithic mistake at scale. Standing context should hold what every task needs; the rest should be discoverable.

Scenarios describe an agent whose context is dominated by tool definitions or procedures, slow or expensive session starts, or wrong-procedure errors as the library grows. The answer moves rarely used capabilities behind discovery (Skills, tool search, just-in-time retrieval, subagents) and keeps the always-loaded part small. When the capability set is small and stable, the answer is the simple monolithic load, often with caching.

Design a RAG pipeline with appropriate chunking and indexing strategies. Design a retrieval pipeline end to end, choosing chunking by the shape of the documents and indexing by how people ask, and keep the index fresh and measured.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) answers questions from a body of knowledge too large, too specialized or too changeable to rely on the model's training. The pipeline has two halves: - Indexing (offline): collect documents, split them into chunks, compute representations, and store them in an index. - Answering (online): turn the question into a query, retrieve candidate chunks, optionally rerank them, and pass the best ones to Claude with instructions to answer from them and cite. Remember lesson 1.2: retrieval is for stable knowledge . Live state comes from tools.

docs.h: Do you need RAG at all?
docs.x: If the whole knowledge base fits comfortably in the context window (a few hundred pages at most), loading it directly, with prompt caching, can be simpler and more accurate than building a pipeline. RAG earns its complexity when the corpus is large, grows, or changes.

docs.h: Chunking: by the shape of the documents
docs.x: The chunk is the unit that comes back. Choose the method by what the documents are, not by a default size. Method How Fits Fixed-size with overlap Equal spans, overlapping a little Uniform, unstructured text with weak natural boundaries Semantic Split where the topic changes Prose, where each chunk must make sense on its own Structural (hierarchical) Follow the document's sections and subsections Manuals, contracts, policies, where the section heading carries meaning A common failure: a chunk loses the context that made it meaningful ("the limit is 30 days", but for which policy?). Fixes include keeping section titles and document names with each chunk, and contextual retrieval , which prepends a short, generated description of where the chunk sits in its document before indexing it.

Index Matches Fits Dense (embeddings) Meaning, even with different words Questions phrased unlike the source text Sparse (keyword, such as BM25) Exact terms: part numbers, codes, names Questions that hinge on a specific identifier Hybrid Both, with results merged Mixed query patterns, which is most production traffic

docs.c: Measure retrieval separately from answers
docs.x: Every retrieval design balances retrieval quality (does the right chunk come back?), latency (how much time retrieval adds) and maintenance (how much it costs to keep the index correct as documents change). Reranking improves quality and adds latency; finer chunking improves precision and increases index size; frequent re-indexing improves freshness and costs compute. Keep a set of questions with the passages that should be retrieved. Track whether the right chunk appears in the top results, not only whether the final answer looks right. A good answer from a lucky retrieval will not stay good.

docs.c: Policies that lost their headings · Tuning retrieval for live data · Default chunk size for every corpus
docs.x: Decide how changes reach the index: re-index changed documents on publish, on a schedule, or both; remove withdrawn documents; record the source version in each chunk so citations point to the right edition. An HR assistant split a 300-page handbook into 500-token chunks. Questions about parental leave sometimes retrieved a paragraph about sick leave, because the chunk ("eligible after 26 weeks...") had lost its section heading. Re-chunking by section, keeping the heading path with each chunk, fixed most of the misses. If the question is about something that changes on its own (stock, order status, balances), no chunking or index choice is the right answer. That data comes from a tool call. Options that apply one fixed chunk size to structured documents (contracts, manuals) without keeping their structure are usually wrong when the scenario mentions answers that mix up sections.

RAG design questions give a corpus and a query pattern, then ask for chunking and indexing choices, or describe a failure (wrong section retrieved, exact codes not found, stale answers) and ask for the fix. Match chunking to document shape, indexing to query pattern (hybrid when identifiers matter), and freshness to how often the documents change. If the corpus is small, consider whether RAG is needed at all.

docs.t: Matching Retrieval to Data and Queries
docs.c: Filter first, rank second
docs.x: - Metadata filters (product, version, region, date, document type) remove whole classes of wrong answers before ranking. - Contextual retrieval adds a short description of each chunk's place in its document before indexing, which reduces misses from context-poor chunks; combined with hybrid search it lowers retrieval failures substantially. - Reranking takes the top few dozen candidates and reorders them with a stronger relevance model, keeping only the best handful. It improves quality and adds latency and cost per query, so it belongs where accuracy matters more than milliseconds. - Query rewriting turns a conversational question into a better search query, using the conversation so far. When the question names a scope (a product, a policy version, a jurisdiction), apply it as a hard filter. Hoping similarity search ranks the right version first is how assistants quote last year's terms.

docs.t: Matching Retrieval to Data and Queries
docs.h: Agentic search versus a one-shot index
docs.c: One assistant, four retrieval methods · Embedding structured records · Reranking everything
docs.x: For codebases, file systems and very large or fast-changing collections, letting an agent search iteratively (list, search, open, follow references) can beat a precomputed index: it always sees the current files and can follow a trail. It is slower and costlier per question, so it suits investigation, not high-volume FAQ answering. An adjuster asks: "Is water damage from a burst pipe covered under this customer's policy, and have we paid a similar claim for them before?" The assistant calls Policy Admin for the customer's policy and its wording version (structured lookup), retrieves the relevant clauses from that wording version only (filtered hybrid search with citations), and queries prior claims for this customer (structured query). The answer quotes the clause and lists the prior claims; the coverage decision stays with the adjuster. Turning database rows into text and searching them by similarity gives fuzzy, stale answers to precise questions. Structured data is queried, not embedded. Reranking adds a model call to every query. For a high-volume, latency-sensitive route where retrieval quality is already adequate, it can be the wrong trade.

Pick the method for each data shape, add filters when the question names a scope, use hybrid search when identifiers matter, add reranking where accuracy outweighs latency, and choose agentic search for codebases or investigative tasks. Distractors apply one method to everything, usually vector search.

Evaluate accuracy-latency trade-offs and justify configuration decisions. Know which configuration settings move accuracy and which move latency, find the setting that holds up the tightest budget, and justify each choice with measurements rather than preference.

Most configuration choices trade accuracy against latency (and usually cost). The architect's job is to know which dial moves which outcome, find the constraint that is actually tight, and defend each setting with numbers.

Setting Effect on accuracy Effect on latency Model tier Larger tiers handle harder reasoning Larger tiers are slower Extended thinking and effort Often better on multi-step problems Adds thinking time and tokens Prompt and context size Relevant context helps; clutter hurts More input takes longer to process Prompt caching No change Faster on cache hits Retrieval depth and reranking More candidates and reranking find better passages Each adds a step Sequential versus parallel tool calls No change Independent calls in parallel finish sooner Output length limits Too short truncates answers Shorter outputs finish sooner Streaming No change Much faster perceived latency: the first words arrive early Batch processing No change Much slower (hours), much cheaper; for work no one waits on

docs.c: Measure the tail under load
docs.x: When a design has both a latency target and an accuracy target, one of them is usually binding. Ask: which setting, if relaxed, would break the tightest budget? That is the setting to protect, and the one to justify most carefully. - If latency is binding: keep thinking low or off, use a faster tier where the evaluation allows, cache the stable prefix, run independent tools in parallel, stream the response, and skip reranking unless retrieval quality demands it. - If accuracy is binding: spend latency where the evaluation shows a gain (a stronger tier, more thinking, reranking) and recover time elsewhere (caching, parallel calls, streaming, fewer retrieved chunks). Latency targets are about the 95th or 99th percentile with realistic concurrency, not one request on a quiet afternoon. Accuracy targets are about the evaluation set, not a demo. Justify every setting with both numbers.

Streaming does not make the full answer arrive sooner, but users see progress within a fraction of a second, which is what most chat experiences need. For a backend step whose output is parsed before anything is shown, streaming does not help; the full time is what counts.

docs.c: Meeting a 3-second target · Streaming as a fix for backend latency · Turning everything up "for quality"
docs.x: One application rarely needs one configuration. A chat route may use a small tier, no thinking and streaming; a nightly analysis job on the same data may use a larger tier, more thinking and batch pricing. Configure per route, not per application. A chat assistant on the balanced tier with thinking enabled had a 95th-percentile response time of 5.8 seconds. The evaluation showed thinking added no measurable accuracy on its question types. Turning thinking off, caching the 6,000-token prefix, calling the order and returns tools in parallel and streaming the reply brought the 95th percentile to 2.4 seconds with first words in under a second, and accuracy unchanged. Options that add streaming to a step whose output must be complete before the next step runs do not reduce the latency that matters. A design that uses the largest tier, maximum thinking and reranking everywhere will rarely meet a real-time target. Spend latency only where the evaluation shows it buys accuracy.

These questions give targets for latency, accuracy and sometimes cost, and a configuration that misses one. Identify the binding constraint, then pick the change that moves it without breaking the others: thinking, tier, caching, parallel tools, streaming, reranking or batch. Answers that justify the change with a measurement on the right percentile are usually the strongest.

Analyze observability challenges and select monitoring strategies at scale. Instrument Claude integrations so any answer can be traced end to end, costs and limits can be attributed to the right team or tenant, and problems are detected before users report them.

When a Claude-powered feature gives a wrong answer at 2 a.m., someone has to find out which model, prompt, inputs, tools and user produced it. At scale, with many routes, tenants and agents, that is impossible without deliberate instrumentation.

docs.h: Log four kinds of information per call
docs.x: Category Fields Request Model and version, prompt template version, input tokens, which tools were offered Response Output tokens, latency (total and time to first token), stop reason, tool calls made Context Trace ID, user role (not raw identity where avoidable), tenant, session, whether the cache was hit Outcome Did the downstream system accept the result? Did the user escalate, correct or rate it? Outcome is the field most often missing, and the one that connects technical behaviour to business results.

docs.c: Version everything that can change behaviour
docs.x: 1. Request tracing. One trace ID follows a request from the gateway through retrieval, every model call, every tool call and every subagent. Standard tracing tools (such as OpenTelemetry) let agent traces join the application's existing traces. 2. Metric aggregation. Latency percentiles, error rates, token use, cost, cache hit rate and outcome rates, per route and per tenant. 3. Anomaly detection. Alerts on changes from the baseline: a jump in escalations, a fall in cache hits, a cost spike for one tenant, a rise in a particular stop reason. 4. Change attribution. Every deploy, prompt version, model change and configuration change is recorded, so a shift in a metric can be tied to its cause. If the logs cannot say which prompt version and model handled a request, a regression cannot be traced to its cause. Prompt and configuration versions belong in every log line.

At scale, you need to know who is using capacity and money, and to stop one consumer from starving others. - Separate keys or workspaces per team, product or tenant let usage, cost and rate limits be tracked and capped separately. One shared key hides who caused a spike, and one heavy tenant can exhaust a limit everyone shares. - Usage and cost reporting by key or workspace feeds chargeback and budget alerts. - Per-tenant dashboards and limits in your own application add a second layer for products that serve many customers.

docs.c: The tenant nobody could see · Logging only errors · Full transcripts by default
docs.x: Logs and traces can become the biggest store of sensitive data in the system. Decide what is recorded: redact or hash personal data, avoid full prompt and response bodies where metadata is enough, restrict access, and set retention to match policy. Trace exporters usually let you control whether message content is included. A SaaS company served 60 customers from one API key. One customer's bulk import loop sent 40,000 requests in an hour, the shared rate limit was hit, and every other customer's assistant began failing. Nobody could tell which customer caused it from the provider's usage view. Moving to per-tenant workspaces with their own limits, and tagging every trace with the tenant ID, made the next incident visible in minutes and confined to the tenant that caused it. Many failures are not errors: the model answers fluently and wrongly, or the user gives up. Without outcome signals, these never show up. Storing every prompt and response verbatim "for debugging" can breach privacy rules and multiply the sensitive data the company holds. Log what is needed, protected and time-limited.

Observability questions describe an incident that could not be diagnosed, a cost or rate-limit problem that could not be attributed, or a multi-agent run whose failure could not be traced. The answer adds the missing piece: trace IDs across components, versioned prompts and models in logs, outcome signals, per-tenant keys or workspaces, or anomaly alerts. Watch for answers that log everything verbatim without regard to privacy.

Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security). Turn "it should work well" into measurable success criteria across accuracy, latency, cost, safety and security, define them before building, and read results by category rather than by a single average.

An evaluation can only be as good as the definition of success behind it. "Good summaries" and "fast enough" cannot be tested. The exam expects you to write criteria that are specific, measurable, achievable and relevant , and to write them before building, so they shape the design rather than excuse it.

Family Example metrics Typical measurement Accuracy and quality Field-level exact match, classification accuracy, faithfulness to source, completeness against a checklist Code checks against labels; rubric graded by a model; human review samples Latency 95th-percentile total time, time to first token Measured under realistic load Cost Cost per request, per successful task, per resolved case Token usage multiplied by price, per route Safety Count of prohibited actions or content, harmful-output rate, correct refusals Code checks where binary; graded review where judgment is needed Security Data leakage across users, injection success rate, unauthorized tool calls Adversarial test cases with code checks

docs.c: Cost per success, not cost per call
docs.x: A usable criterion names the metric, the target, the population and the measurement method: - Weak: "The assistant should be accurate." - Strong: "At least 95% of extracted claim amounts exactly match the source document, measured on the 400-claim test set, with no category below 90%." Some criteria are thresholds (must be met to ship), some are guardrails (must not get worse), and some are zero-tolerance (any occurrence fails): "no claim is ever denied automatically", "no customer ever sees another customer's data". Zero-tolerance criteria are usually checked with code, not with judgment. A cheaper configuration that fails more often can cost more per resolved case once retries, escalations and human rework are counted. Measure cost against the business outcome.

Averages hide regressions. Report results for each category of input (normal, edge cases, adversarial, each product line or language) as well as overall. A change that lifts common cases a little and breaks a rare but important case badly can still raise the average. Slice Before After Routine requests (80% of traffic) 92% 95% Requests mentioning a legal dispute (5%) 88% 61% Overall 91% 91% The overall number is unchanged; the change is a regression on the slice that matters most.

docs.h: Connect technical metrics to business ones
docs.c: Criteria for a contract summarizer · "Measure quality with user thumbs-up" · One overall score
docs.x: Every technical metric should map to something the business recognizes: task success to resolved cases, 95th-percentile latency to customer waiting time, override rate to staff workload, cost per success to operating cost. Reporting only token savings, without the business effect, invites the wrong decision. Accuracy: every obligation with a deadline appears in the summary (checked against a labelled list, at least 97%). Faithfulness: no statement unsupported by the contract (model-graded rubric, calibrated on 100 human-reviewed cases, at least 98%). Latency: 95th percentile under 20 seconds for contracts up to 80 pages. Cost: under $0.40 per contract. Security: zero instances of content from one client's contracts appearing in another's summary. User ratings are a useful signal, but they are sparse, biased and arrive after launch. They cannot replace criteria defined and tested before release. Options that accept a change because the average improved, without checking the slices, are distractors when the scenario mentions edge cases or high-risk categories.

Metric questions ask which criterion is well formed, which measurement fits a requirement, or whether a result justifies a release. Strong answers are specific and measurable, include the measurement method, use code checks for binary safety and security rules, measure latency at a high percentile, express cost per successful outcome, and look at category-level results.

Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies. Build a golden dataset that reflects real traffic and its hard cases, and grade it with the cheapest reliable method for each behaviour: code first, a calibrated model judge where interpretation is needed, and people where stakes or novelty demand it.
An evaluation framework has two parts: what you test (the dataset) and how you score it (the graders). Getting either wrong produces numbers that look reassuring and mean little.

docs.c: The dataset grows with the system
docs.x: A golden dataset is a set of realistic inputs with expected outputs or grading criteria, used to judge every version of the system on the same footing. A useful one covers: Category Example for a claims assistant Typical cases A routine auto claim with all documents Edge cases A claim with two vehicles and three policy holders Ambiguous inputs A description that fits two claim types Invalid or incomplete inputs No policy number; unreadable scan Adversarial inputs Text that tries to change the assistant's instructions Boundary conditions The longest documents the system must handle Negative cases Requests the system should refuse or escalate Real production data is the best source of inputs (anonymized as required), weighted to match real traffic, with extra cases for rare but important categories. Synthetic cases fill gaps, especially for adversarial and boundary conditions. Every production failure, every user correction and every new feature adds cases. A static test set drifts away from reality and stops catching regressions. Keep two kinds of suite: capability tests that track progress on what the system cannot yet do well, and regression tests that protect behaviour that already works and must stay working.

Choose the cheapest grader that is reliable for each behaviour. Grader Use for Strengths Limits Code Formats, schemas, exact values, banned actions, latency, cost Fast, cheap, deterministic Cannot judge meaning or tone Model judge Faithfulness, completeness, tone, reasoning quality Scales; handles nuance Costs money; can be inconsistent; must itself be validated Human review High-stakes, novel or disputed judgments; calibrating the judge The reference standard Slow, expensive, hard to scale One system usually uses all three: code checks on every case, a model judge on the interpretive criteria, and humans on a sample and on anything the judge flags as uncertain.

- Give it a detailed rubric with clear definitions and examples of each grade. - Ask for constrained verdicts (a small set of labels such as pass, minor issue, fail) rather than open-ended scores. - Ask it to give its reasoning before the verdict , and grade one criterion at a time. - Calibrate against a set of human-graded cases and track agreement over time. - Prefer a different model or configuration from the one being graded, to reduce bias toward its own style.

docs.c: One requirement, three graders · A judge where a parser would do · A dataset of clean, typical cases
docs.x: Model outputs vary between runs. Run important cases more than once, and look at pass rates across runs rather than a single result, especially for agents whose paths can differ. "The summary lists every medication change with the correct dose" is checked in code against the structured medication record. "The summary is faithful to the notes" is graded by a model judge with a rubric. "The summary is clinically safe to send" is reviewed by a physician on a weekly sample and on every case the judge rates as uncertain. Options that use a model judge to check whether output is valid JSON, within length or free of a banned field are wasteful and less reliable than code. A test set without edge, adversarial and negative cases overstates quality. Prefer the option that adds them, weighted to their real importance.

Framework questions ask what the dataset should contain, which grader fits a requirement, or how to make a judge reliable. Strong answers cover hard and adversarial cases, keep the dataset growing from production, apply code first, use a calibrated rubric-based judge for interpretation, and reserve human review for high stakes and calibration.

Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements. Prove that a change improves a live system with a properly designed experiment, choose shadow testing when users must not see the new version, and roll out in stages with clear stop rules.

Offline evaluations tell you whether a change meets criteria on a test set. They cannot tell you how real users and real traffic respond. For that you run a controlled experiment on live traffic, or, when exposure is too risky, a shadow test.

1. Offline evaluation on the golden dataset: does the change meet the thresholds and keep the regression suite green? 2. Shadow test where risk is high: the new version processes copies of real requests; only the current version's output reaches users. 3. A/B test (or a small canary) where some exposure is acceptable: a random share of users gets the new version. 4. Staged rollout with monitoring and a rollback trigger. Each step answers a different question. Skipping straight to an A/B test for a high-risk change, or treating an offline score as proof of user impact, are both mistakes.

docs.h: Five parts of a sound A/B test
docs.x: Part What to get right Hypothesis Specific and falsifiable: the change, the expected effect, the primary metric, and the constraints that must hold Assignment Random, and sticky per user or session, so groups are comparable and no one sees both versions Primary metric One metric, chosen before the test. Guardrail metrics (latency, cost, safety) must not get worse Sample size Enough traffic to detect the smallest effect worth acting on, at the confidence the stakes demand Interpretation Judge against the hypothesis set in advance; do not stop early on a promising trend or go looking for a metric that improved A hypothesis that works: "Moving product questions to the small tier will cut cost per resolved contact by at least 30%, while resolution rate falls by no more than 2 points and 95th-percentile latency does not rise."

docs.c: Decide the stop rule before you start
docs.x: The smaller the difference you want to detect, the more data you need, roughly in proportion to the square of how small it is. A rough rule for a rate (such as resolution) at 95% confidence and 80% power: samples per group ≈ 16 × p × (1 − p) ÷ d² , where p is the baseline rate and d the difference to detect. At a 70% baseline, detecting a 5-point change needs about 16 × 0.21 ÷ 0.0025 ≈ 1,350 per group ; detecting a 2-point change needs about 8,400 per group . Model outputs vary more than traditional software, which pushes these numbers up. Higher stakes call for higher confidence and therefore more data. Fix the sample size or duration, the primary metric and the guardrails in advance. Stopping when the numbers look good, or extending until they do, turns noise into false conclusions.

Situation Approach A single bad output could cause real harm (clinical, legal, financial) Shadow test first Not enough traffic to split Shadow test, then a small canary Some exposure is acceptable and user behaviour is what matters A/B test You need to know how users react (satisfaction, conversion, escalation) A/B test, since shadow outputs never reach users Shadow tests compare outputs on real inputs, usually with graders and human review. They cannot measure user reactions.

docs.c: Shadow first, then a canary · Choosing the metric after the results · Non-random groups
docs.x: Every experiment should leave the system better instrumented: new failure cases go into the golden dataset, and the winning version becomes the new control. Improvement is a loop, not a launch. A bank wants a new model for summarizing customer complaints that feed regulatory reporting. It runs the new version in shadow on two weeks of real complaints, grades both versions' outputs side by side, and has compliance review 200 pairs. The new version wins on completeness with no omissions of regulated facts, so it goes to 10% of complaints for two weeks with a rollback trigger on reviewer corrections, then to everyone. Options that pick whichever metric improved, or that stop the test early because the first days look good, are distractors. Giving the new version to "the simpler queries" or "the friendliest customers" makes it look better than it is. Assignment must be random.

Experiment questions give a proposed change, traffic volumes and a risk level. Choose offline evaluation first, shadow testing for high-risk changes or low traffic, and A/B testing when user behaviour must be measured and exposure is acceptable. Check that the hypothesis, primary metric and stop rule were set in advance, assignment is random and sticky, and the sample is large enough for the effect size.

Diagnose system issues (prompt failure, hallucinations, model mismatch). Classify a production problem before fixing it, telling prompt failures, hallucinations, model mismatches, retrieval failures and orchestration failures apart, and apply the first action that fits the cause.

When an AI system misbehaves, the tempting fix is the biggest lever: a new model, a longer prompt. The exam rewards the opposite habit: classify the failure first , then apply the smallest fix that addresses its cause.

Failure What you see Typical cause First action Prompt failure Inconsistent format or behaviour; the model does something reasonable but not what was wanted Ambiguous or missing instructions Make the instruction specific; add an output contract or examples Hallucination Fluent, confident, unsupported facts (prices, dates, policy terms, citations) The model was not given the facts, or not told to rely only on them Ground it: tool call or retrieval for the facts; allow "I don't know"; require citations Retrieval failure Answers based on the wrong passage, or "not found" when the answer exists Chunking, index or filter problems Inspect what was retrieved; fix chunking, filters or index type Model mismatch Consistently shallow or incomplete work on hard cases; fine on easy ones Tier too small for the task (or too slow or costly for it) Evaluate another tier on the failing slice Context problem Quality degrades late in long sessions; truncated outputs Cluttered or overflowing context Trim, compact, or split the work (lesson 2.4) Orchestration failure Incomplete reports, missing pieces, silent gaps in multi-agent output A subagent failed and synthesis carried on Trace across agents; validate results; reconcile coverage Integration failure Errors, timeouts, empty tool results treated as answers Downstream outage, bad tool error handling Retries, clear tool errors, fallbacks

docs.c: Smallest fix for the classified cause · Three symptoms, three causes · Upgrading the model as a first resort · Fixing hallucinations with sterner instructions
docs.x: - Read the trace , not the summary: what was in the context, which tools ran, what they returned, what the stop reason was. A response cut off at the output limit is not a reasoning problem. - Find the slice. Does it fail on all inputs or a category (long documents, one product line, one language)? A slice-specific failure points to data, retrieval or model fit; a universal one points to the prompt or configuration. - Check what changed. Prompt version, model version, index refresh, tool change. Most sudden regressions follow a change. - Reproduce, then fix, then add a test. Every diagnosed failure becomes a case in the golden dataset. Wrong facts call for grounding, not a bigger model. Vague output calls for a clearer prompt, not more context. A failed subagent calls for validation at synthesis, not a stronger orchestrator. A support assistant (1) quotes a return window of 60 days when policy says 30, (2) sometimes answers in a paragraph and sometimes in bullet points, and (3) gives weak answers only on furniture assembly questions. The trace shows (1) no policy passage was retrieved, so the model filled the gap: a grounding and retrieval fix. (2) The prompt never specified a format: a prompt fix. (3) Assembly manuals were chunked without step context: a chunking fix. None of the three needed a model change. When a scenario shows wrong facts or inconsistent formatting, "move to a more capable model" is usually the distractor. Classify first. "Do not make things up" helps a little. Giving the model the facts, and permission to say it does not know, helps a lot.

Diagnosis questions describe a symptom, sometimes with log details, and offer fixes. Map the symptom to a failure type using the evidence (what was retrieved, the stop reason, which slice fails, what changed recently), then pick the first action that addresses that cause. The model change is rarely the first answer.

Monitor system performance using logging and observability tools. Keep watching quality, latency and cost after launch, using logs, sampled online evaluation, outcome signals and alerts, and feed what you find back into the evaluation set.

A system that passed its evaluation can still drift in production: the inputs change, documents are updated, users find new ways to ask, upstream systems change their formats. Monitoring is how you notice before customers or auditors do.

Area Signals Quality Sampled online evaluation scores, human-review outcomes, user corrections, escalation and override rates Reliability Error rates, timeouts, tool failures, stop reasons (especially output-limit and context-exceeded), retries Latency 50th and 95th percentile total time and time to first token, per route Cost Tokens and cost per request and per successful outcome, cache hit rate, per route and per tenant Safety and security Guardrail triggers, blocked actions, injection attempts detected, policy violations found in review

Offline test sets do not see this week's traffic. Online evaluation grades a sample of real production outputs with the same graders: code checks on everything that can be checked cheaply, a model judge on a sample, and human review on a smaller sample plus anything flagged. Trends in these scores are the earliest warning of drift.

A useful habit is to sort reviewed outputs into three bins: - Acceptable : meets the criteria. - Needs revision : fixable by regenerating or editing. - Needs override : a person or a different path must take over. The rates of each bin, by route and slice, show where the system is weakening. Every "needs override" case is a candidate for the golden dataset.

docs.c: Pin versions so changes are deliberate
docs.x: Alert on changes from a baseline , sized to matter, sustained for long enough to rule out noise: escalation rate up 4 points for a day, cost per success up 30% for an hour, 95th-percentile latency over target for 15 minutes, any zero-tolerance violation at once. Each alert needs an owner and a first step. Use specific model versions rather than moving aliases in production, and record prompt and configuration versions with every request. Then every shift in a metric can be tied to a change you made, or ruled out as one.

docs.c: A drift nobody deployed · Monitoring only uptime and errors · Floating model aliases in production
docs.x: Monitoring that only produces dashboards changes nothing. The loop is: detect, diagnose (lesson 4.4), fix, add the case to the evaluation set, and confirm the metric recovers. A product assistant's sampled faithfulness score fell from 96% to 89% over three weeks with no code, prompt or model change. Change attribution showed the help-centre team had restructured 80 articles into longer pages, and the chunking no longer split them well. Re-chunking restored the score, and the content team's publishing checklist gained a step to notify the AI team of structural changes. A system that answers every request quickly and wrongly is green on an error dashboard. Quality and outcome signals must be monitored too. If the model behind an alias changes, behaviour can shift without any change on your side. Production should pin versions and upgrade deliberately through evaluation.

Monitoring questions describe a quality drop, a cost spike or a silent change, and ask what should have caught it or what to add. Strong answers include online evaluation on sampled traffic, outcome signals, baselines with meaningful thresholds, pinned and logged versions, and a loop back into the evaluation set.

Optimize token usage, latency, and cost-performance trade-offs. Find where the tokens, time and money actually go, then apply the levers in order of value: trim and cache, right-size the model and thinking, restructure long-running work, and batch what can wait, without giving up the quality bar.

Optimization is the Domain 4 counterpart to design: the system works, and now it must cost less, respond faster or both, without falling below the quality bar . Every optimization is a change, so it goes through the same evaluation gate as any other.

Before changing anything, break cost and latency down: - by route (which features cost the most?), - by component (system prompt, tool definitions, retrieved context, conversation history, tool results, output, thinking), - by distribution (is the bill driven by typical requests or by a long tail of huge ones?). Agents deserve special attention: context that grows turn by turn means the later turns cost far more than the early ones, and a few long sessions can dominate the bill.

docs.h: Step 2: apply levers in order of value
docs.c: Optimize cost per success
docs.x: Lever Saves Quality risk Remove what is not needed (unused tools, repeated instructions, whole documents where a section would do) Tokens, latency Low Cache stable prefixes Input cost and latency None Trim and summarize tool results; clear stale ones; compact long sessions Tokens in long sessions Low, if identifiers are preserved Limit output length; ask for structure instead of prose Output tokens, latency Low Right-size thinking (effort or budget) Output tokens, latency Evaluate Right-size the model per route or step (route easy work to a smaller tier) Cost, latency Evaluate Batch work that can wait About half the cost None, but slower Parallelize independent calls Latency None The first rows are nearly free; the later ones need evaluation evidence. A configuration that halves cost per call but doubles escalations or retries has not saved money. Measure cost against the business outcome, and keep the quality metrics as guardrails on every optimization.

docs.c: An agent whose context grew without limit · Optimizing the average · Saving money by dropping quality controls
docs.x: Run the evaluation suite before and after, compare by slice, and watch the production metrics after rollout. Add a budget alert so a later change that undoes the saving is noticed. An internal research agent averaged 35 turns per task. Because every tool result stayed in its history, input per turn grew from 8,000 to 140,000 tokens, and the last ten turns cost more than the first twenty-five together. Clearing tool results once summarized into notes, capping each tool's response size, and caching the stable instructions cut cost per task by about 70% with no change in the evaluation score. Cutting a few tokens from every typical request does little when a small share of very long requests drives most of the cost. Find the distribution first. Removing validation steps, the human review gate or the evaluation run to save cost is not optimization. Those controls are part of the requirement.

Optimization questions give a cost or latency problem and several changes. Prefer the change that targets the measured driver with the least quality risk (trimming, caching, managing agent context, output limits), then evidence-backed model and thinking changes, then batch for work that can wait. Reject options that skip evaluation, remove safety controls, or optimize a part of the bill that is not the problem.

Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems. Know what model training covers and what the architect owns, recognize the recurring risk classes of LLM systems, and assess a proposed design for them before it ships.

Claude is trained to refuse clearly harmful requests and to behave safely in general. That is valuable, and it is not the same as your application being safe. The model knows nothing about your refund policy, your customers' data rules or which actions your users may take.

Layer Owner Covers Does not cover Trained behaviour Anthropic Broad classes of harmful content, baseline safety Your business rules, data policies, permissions System prompt Architect Role, tone, task rules Enforcement against adversarial or unusual input Runtime screening Architect Checking inputs and outputs for disallowed content Authorizing actions; every novel attack Authorization Architect Whether this caller may do this action now Content quality, fairness Any rule specific to your organization, its data or its actions has to live in a layer the architect controls.

Risk What it looks like Primary mitigation Hallucination Confident, unsupported facts Ground in tools and retrieval; allow "I don't know"; cite sources Direct prompt injection A user tells the model to ignore its instructions Screening, clear separation of instructions and input, least privilege Indirect prompt injection Instructions hidden in documents, emails, web pages or tool results Treat all retrieved content as untrusted data; no dangerous capability for it to trigger Tool and action abuse The model is induced to call a side-effecting tool outside policy Authorization before execution; approval for consequential actions Data exposure Personal or confidential data in context, outputs or logs where it should not be Minimize what enters context; redact logs; scope retrieval to the user Context and budget exhaustion Oversized inputs push out instructions or crowd out the answer Input limits, token counting, chunking Prompt and configuration leakage The system prompt or internal details are extracted Keep secrets out of prompts; do not rely on prompt secrecy Over-reliance People accept outputs without checking Review designed into the workflow; visible sources and uncertainty

docs.c: Assume the model can be fooled
docs.x: Some failure modes need no attacker: stale knowledge, weak arithmetic, inconsistency between runs, degraded quality in very long contexts, and behaviour shifts between model versions. Design for them as you would for any known component limitation. Design so that a fully manipulated model still cannot do serious harm: it cannot reach data the user may not see, cannot take actions the user may not take, and cannot act irreversibly without approval.

docs.c: A summarizer that could send email · "Claude is trained to be safe, so we are covered" · Screening only the user's message
docs.x: Walk the request path from input to action and ask at each step: what untrusted content enters here, what could the model be induced to do, what happens if it is wrong, and what stops it? Record each risk with its likelihood, impact and the control that addresses it. A team's meeting-notes assistant reads shared documents and can send follow-up emails. A shared document contains hidden text asking the assistant to email the quarterly forecast to an outside address. Training may well resist; the design should not depend on it. Removing external recipients from the email tool, and requiring the user to confirm every send, closes the risk regardless of what the model is persuaded to do. Options that rely on model training for business rules, data rules or permissions are wrong. Training is one layer; the architect owns the rest. In retrieval and agent designs, much of the untrusted text comes from documents and tool results. Defences that only look at the user's input miss indirect injection.

Risk questions give a design and ask what the biggest risk is, or which control addresses a stated risk. Identify the risk class (especially indirect injection in retrieval and agent designs), then choose controls the architect owns and that hold even if the model is manipulated: least privilege, authorization before actions, approval for irreversible steps, grounding, and data minimization.

Implement guardrails and safety controls. Place guardrails at the three control points (input, output and action authorization), choose model-based or deterministic checks for each, chain them, and decide what each does when it fails.
Guardrails are runtime controls the architect adds around the model. The exam focuses on where they sit, what kind of check each one is, and what happens when the check itself fails .

docs.c: Output filters cannot undo actions
docs.x: Control point When Question it answers Typical checks Input screening Before the model call Should this content reach the model at all? Length and format limits, known-bad patterns, a classifier for jailbreak or injection attempts, PII redaction Output screening Before the response reaches a person or system Is this output safe and compliant to deliver? Schema validation, forbidden fields or phrases, policy and toxicity checks, grounding checks Action authorization Before any tool with side effects runs Is this caller allowed to do this, here, now? Identity, permission, scope, limits, approval status Input screening covers retrieved documents and tool results too, not only what the user typed. If a tool call can move money, change records or send messages, the check must run before the tool executes . Screening the text of the final response happens after the refund has already been issued.

Check Use when Example Deterministic (code, rules, schemas, allowlists) The rule is exact and must be predictable and auditable Refund over limit, banned field present, caller lacks permission Model-based (a classifier or judge) Detection needs language understanding and the patterns are open-ended A cleverly worded jailbreak, a policy-violating tone Authorization is always deterministic. Model-based checks fail differently (they miss novel patterns and sometimes flag harmless ones), so chain them with deterministic checks rather than relying on either alone. A fast, small model often works well as a first-pass screen.

Every guardrail is a dependency that can itself fail: a timeout, an outage, a crash. - Fail closed: if the check cannot run, the request or action is blocked (or queued) until it can. - Fail open: if the check cannot run, the request proceeds unchecked. Safety-critical gates, and anything protecting money, data or irreversible actions, fail closed. Fail-open is acceptable only for low-risk, advisory checks, and should still be logged and alerted, because a silently failing guardrail gives the appearance of protection with none of the effect.

docs.c: The refund that slipped through · Treating output screening as the safety net · Fail-open for availability
docs.x: Log every block and every check failure with the reason. Rising block rates may mean an attack or an over-sensitive rule; falling rates after a change may mean a check stopped running. An assistant could call a refund tool. The team added an output filter to catch responses promising refunds. During testing, a crafted message led the model to call the refund tool directly; the refund was issued, and the output filter later flagged the text. The fix was an authorization check inside the refund service (caller, order ownership, amount, approval), failing closed if the check could not be completed. Options that rely on an output filter to stop a side-effecting action are wrong. Authorization comes before the action. "Let requests through if the safety service is down, so customers are not blocked" is the wrong answer for any control that protects money, data or safety.

Guardrail questions describe a request path and an incident or requirement. Place each check at the right point, pick deterministic checks for exact rules and authorization and model-based checks for open-ended language risks, and choose fail-closed for consequential controls. Watch for designs that screen only user input, or that check the response after the action has happened.

Block and fail-closed counts per check per day, with alerts on sudden rises (possible attack or broken rule) and on drops to zero (a check that may have stopped running); a weekly review of a sample of blocked claims for false positives. - Attachments and OCR text are screened, not only email bodies. - Decision language is checked by code before sending. - Payment and denial are impossible, not just blocked by a filter. - Failures route to handlers, not straight through.

Apply human-in-the-loop validation strategies. Route decisions to people by stakes rather than by volume, place the review where it protects against the real harm, and design the reviewer's job so oversight stays meaningful instead of becoming a rubber stamp.
"Put a human in the loop" is not a design. The questions are which decisions need a person, where in the flow the person sits, and what they need to do the job well.

docs.h: Route by stakes, not by volume
docs.c: The routing rule
docs.x: Three properties of a decision set the need for review: - Reversibility: can a wrong decision be undone cheaply? A draft email can; a sent payment or a denied benefit often cannot. - Cost of a wrong decision: a mislabelled ticket costs little; a wrong clinical or financial decision costs a lot. - Confidence: how likely the system is to be wrong on this case. Confidence is only useful if it is calibrated against real outcomes; a model can be confidently wrong. Send a decision to a person when confidence is low and the decision is irreversible or costly. High-stakes decisions may need review even at high confidence; low-stakes, reversible ones usually do not need it at all. Confidence Reversible? Cost of error Review High Yes Low None; monitor Low Yes Low None or sampled; monitor High No High Often still required, or sampled at a high rate Low No High Always, before the action

Placement How it works Fits Cost Pre-action approval Nothing happens until a person approves Irreversible or high-cost actions Latency and reviewer capacity Post-action audit The action happens; a person reviews afterwards and can reverse it Reversible, lower-cost actions at volume Errors take effect before they are caught Sampled review A share of decisions is reviewed to measure quality Monitoring routine work Individual errors can slip through Many systems combine them: pre-approval for the risky band, post-action audit for the middle, sampling for the rest.

docs.c: Expense approvals · "Send everything to a human to be safe" · Confidence as the only trigger
docs.x: Sending everything to people looks safe and fails in practice. Reviewers facing long queues of routine approvals start approving without reading ( consent fatigue or approval fatigue), so the risky cases get the least attention. Design the reviewer's job: - Route only what needs judgment, so each review matters. - Show the evidence : the inputs, the sources the system used, why it was flagged, and what the system recommends. - Make disagreeing easy, and record overrides with a reason. - Track reviewer agreement and time per case; a fall in review time with rising volume is a warning sign. - Feed overrides back into evaluation (lesson 4.5). Diligence is the human counterpart: the reviewer remains accountable for what they approve, which only works if the system gives them what they need to judge. A company's expense assistant checks receipts against policy. Claims under $100 that match policy are approved automatically and 5% are sampled. Claims under $1,000 that match policy are paid, then audited weekly. Anything over $1,000, or with a policy mismatch, waits for a manager, who sees the receipt, the matched policy clause and the reason for the flag. Managers now review 6% of claims instead of all of them, and spend longer on each. This fails at scale through consent fatigue and delay. The better option routes by stakes and gives reviewers evidence. A design that skips review for any high-confidence decision ignores stakes. An irreversible, high-cost action can deserve review even when the model is confident.

Review questions give a decision type, volume, reversibility and cost, and ask which cases go to a person and when. Apply the routing rule, pick pre-action approval for irreversible or high-cost actions, post-action audit or sampling for reversible ones, and prefer designs that give reviewers evidence and avoid flooding them.

Ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP). Turn regulatory obligations such as HIPAA, GDPR, data residency and FedRAMP into a control register where every obligation has a technical control, an accountable owner and evidence that it works.

Compliance for AI systems is not a statement in a design document. It is a set of controls that can be shown to work. The exam expects you to know the main regimes at an architect's level and, above all, to connect each obligation to something enforceable and provable.

Regime Applies to What it means for the architecture HIPAA US protected health information handled for covered entities A Business Associate Agreement must cover the specific service and configuration; features outside that coverage (often beta features) cannot touch PHI GDPR Personal data of people in the EU A lawful basis, data minimization, a data processing agreement, rights such as access and erasure, and lawful mechanisms for transfers outside the EU Data residency Contractual, regulatory or internal rules on where data is processed and stored The model's processing location and every copy : logs, caches, traces, backups, vector stores FedRAMP US federal cloud workloads Only routes authorized at the required impact level qualify Sector and internal rules Financial, legal, public sector, company policy Approved vendors and routes, retention periods, privilege and audit requirements Note that GDPR does not by itself demand that data stay in the EU; an explicit residency requirement does. Read the requirement in the scenario carefully.

docs.c: A control without evidence is an assertion
docs.x: For every obligation, record four things: Field Question Obligation What must be true? Control What enforces it, technically? Owner Who is accountable for keeping it working? Evidence What artifact proves it works, and when was it last checked? Obligation Control Owner Evidence PHI only through BAA-covered services Route and feature allowlist in the gateway; non-covered features disabled Security lead Signed BAA, gateway configuration, quarterly config export Data stays in the approved region Regional deployment for model calls, storage, logs, caches and vector store Data owner Data-flow record showing every copy; configuration screenshots; test results Decisions can be explained Decision logs with inputs, retrieved sources, outputs, routing and approver Architect A real decision reconstructed from production logs Retention limits Automatic deletion jobs Platform owner Deletion job reports "We comply with HIPAA" is not a control. A gateway allowlist that blocks non-covered features, owned by a named person, with a configuration export from last quarter, is.

Configurations drift, vendors add features, new routes appear, and evidence goes stale. Re-validate the register on a schedule and after every significant change (a new model, a new feature, a new data source).

docs.c: Residency beyond the model call · "The provider is certified, so we are compliant" · Residency checked only at inference
docs.x: Check compliance before choosing the integration route. A route that fails a regulatory or procurement requirement is ruled out regardless of its technical merits (lesson 3.1). A European insurer configured its model calls to run in an EU region and declared residency met. An audit found that the observability vendor stored full request traces in the US, and the vector database's backups replicated to another continent. The fix was a data-flow record listing every copy of claim data, with each location configured and evidenced. A provider's certification or a general agreement does not make every configuration compliant. The specific route, features and data flows must be covered. Logs, caches, traces, backups and embeddings are copies of the data. A residency control that covers only the model call is incomplete.

Compliance questions describe a regulated workload and offer designs or evidence. Strong answers select a route covered for the exact configuration, account for every copy of the data, and map obligations to controls, owners and evidence. Distractors rely on prompt instructions ("handle PHI carefully"), general certifications, or documentation without proof.

Address ethical AI considerations (bias, fairness, transparency). Find the points where an AI system can treat people unequally, measure outcomes by group where lawful, and log decisions so each one can be explained to the person affected, an auditor and an engineer.

Fairness is not something an organization can hand to its model provider. Even a carefully trained model sits inside a system of data, prompts, examples and routing rules, and unequal treatment can enter at any of them.

Injection point How bias gets in Example Data and retrieval The sources over- or under-represent groups, or encode past unequal decisions A hiring assistant retrieves past "successful employee" profiles from a period of skewed hiring Prompt framing Wording carries assumptions A prompt describing "typical reliable applicants" in ways that correlate with background Examples Few-shot examples come from one group or reflect historical bias Every example of an approved application has the same profile Inputs and processing Some groups' inputs are handled worse Handwritten or non-native-language submissions extracted less accurately, then treated as incomplete Routing and thresholds Different groups are sent down different paths One group's cases escalated for extra scrutiny more often for the same facts Measuring only the final answer misses most of these. Fairness has to be checked wherever the system retrieves, interprets, classifies or routes.

- Outcome rates by group , where collecting or inferring group data is lawful and done with suitable protections: approval rates, escalation rates, time to decision, error rates. - Counterfactual tests : run the same case with only a group-related detail changed (a name, an age, a neighbourhood) and check that the outcome does not change when it should not. - Slice the evaluation set (lesson 4.1) by the groups and input types that matter, and treat a gap as a regression. Anthropic's own research on discrimination in model decisions uses this kind of approach: systematic variations of the same scenario to reveal differences in treatment.

If a decision cannot be reconstructed, it cannot be explained or investigated. For each decision, keep: - the original inputs, - the retrieved context that influenced it, - the model's output and the configuration (model, prompt version), - the routing decision and any human action, - an identifier linking all of these. Different audiences need different explanations: Audience Needs The affected person Why this decision was made about them, in plain language, and how to contest it Regulator or auditor Evidence that the required process and controls were followed Engineers Inputs, context, configuration and path, to reproduce and fix

docs.c: Check fairness at every decision point, not just the answer · Slower service for handwritten claims · "The model is unbiased, so the system is fair" · An aggregate accuracy figure
docs.x: Reviewers and operators should judge outputs rather than accept them: is this decision justified by the evidence, is the same rule applied consistently, does anything suggest the outcome turned on an irrelevant characteristic? This habit, called discernment in Anthropic's AI Fluency framework, is what turns logging into accountability. Ask, for each step that retrieves, classifies or routes: could this treat comparable people differently? Then measure it. An insurer's intake system extracted typed claims well and handwritten ones poorly. Low-confidence handwritten claims went to a manual queue that took three days longer. Older customers, who submitted more handwritten claims, were waiting longer on average. No one had designed unfairness; a processing gap plus a routing rule produced it. Improving OCR, and giving the manual queue the same SLA, closed the gap; the slice now appears in every evaluation. Options that delegate fairness to the model provider miss the injection points the architect controls: data, prompts, examples, processing and routing. A single accuracy number can hide large differences between groups. Prefer options that measure by subgroup and by input type.

Fairness and transparency questions describe a decision system and an observed or potential disparity, or a request to explain a decision. Locate the injection point, choose measurement by group or counterfactual testing, and make sure decisions are logged well enough to reconstruct. Distractors rely on the provider's training, a disclaimer, or overall averages.

docs.h: Apply it: Check Prairie State's claim prioritization for fairness
docs.x: Prairie State wants a queue score so the most urgent claims reach adjusters first (see the case). The proposal: Claude reads each claim and scores urgency from 1 to 5 using the description, the attachments and the customer's claim history; the highest scores are assessed first. 1. Find the injection points where comparable customers could be treated differently. Done when: you have at least four, including one in processing and one in routing. 2. Redesign the scoring to reduce them. 3. Define the measurements that would show the score is fair. 4. Define the decision log that lets Prairie State explain a customer's queue position. 1. Injection points - Inputs and processing: handwritten and scanned claims, and claims written in non-native English, are extracted less accurately, so injuries or uninhabitable homes may be missed. - Prompt framing: "urgency" left undefined lets the model reward articulate, emotional descriptions over terse ones. - Data: claim history as a factor penalizes customers who have claimed before, unrelated to current urgency. - Routing: a low score means waiting longer, which compounds any of the above. - Examples: if examples of urgent claims come from one channel (web forms), others look less urgent. 2. Redesign. Define urgency as explicit criteria (injury, uninhabitable home, vulnerable occupant, vehicle needed for medical travel), extracted as structured yes/no fields with the supporting text quoted. Code computes the score from those fields, not the model. Claim history is excluded. Low-confidence extractions are flagged for a quick human check rather than scored low. Examples cover every channel. 3. Measurements. Time to first adjuster contact and score distributions by channel (email, web, mail) and by language of submission; counterfactual tests rewriting the same claim tersely, emotionally, handwritten and typed, which should get the same score; and the share of truly urgent claims (judged by adjusters afterwards) that were scored urgent, by channel. 4. Decision log. Claim ID, inputs and attachments references, extracted urgency fields with quoted evidence, extraction confidence, the score and the rule version that computed it, queue position over time, and any human change with its reason. Customer-facing explanation: which urgency criteria applied and how to tell Prairie State if something urgent was missed. - I found an injection point in processing and one in routing. - The score is computed by code from explicit criteria. - Claim history no longer affects urgency. - I measure by channel and run counterfactual tests.

Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering. Run discovery as structured elicitation, turn what stakeholders say into requirements, constraints and assumptions, and write it down so every design decision traces back to a source.

Stakeholders describe what they want in their own language: "seamless", "accurate", "safe with our data". Each phrase hides a requirement the architecture must meet, and different readings lead to different designs. Discovery is the work of finding out which.

1. Listen for the goal in the stakeholder's words, and for the expectations they did not say aloud. 2. Translate each statement into a requirement, a constraint, or an open question. 3. Write it down : requirements with their source, assumptions marked as assumptions, decisions with their reason. Skipping the third step is how an unstated assumption survives design, build and testing, and surfaces in production or an audit, when changing course is most expensive.

docs.h: Four questions that structure a discovery session
docs.x: Question Establishes Example answers What must it do? Functional scope Draft the summary; check the policy; route the request What must it not do? Boundaries Never send without approval; never touch payment data What must it cost? Budget and capacity Run cost per month; acceptable cost per case; staff time What must it prove? Evidence and audit Who approved each output; that data stayed in region

Stakeholder says Implied constraint Architectural consequence "It has to feel instant" A latency target, and graceful behaviour when slow Agree a 95th-percentile target; stream responses; define the fallback "Just read the form and send it to the right team" Routing is a business rule Claude extracts; a rules engine routes "Someone will check it anyway" A human approval step exists Make the approval gate mandatory and designed, not assumed "We are a bank, so be careful" Regulatory and audit obligations Identify the specific obligations; plan controls and evidence

docs.c: Every requirement has a source
docs.x: A requirement traces to something a stakeholder stated or an obligation that was confirmed. An assumption is something the architect believes but nobody has confirmed: a retention period, a volume, that a system has an API, that users will accept a delay. Assumptions are fine; unlabelled assumptions are not. Record each one with who can confirm it and by when, and treat confirming it as work. If you cannot point to the person or document a requirement came from, it is an assumption. Label it, and go and confirm it.

docs.c: "Make it accurate" · Designing from the first sentence · Assumptions written as requirements
docs.x: A good discovery produces a short set of artifacts the design depends on: the translation table, the requirements list with sources, the assumption register, the success criteria (lesson 4.1), and the constraints that rule options out (regulation, approved vendors, budgets, latency). A legal team asked for "an accurate contract assistant". Discovery found three different meanings: the deal team wanted every obligation and deadline captured (completeness), the general counsel wanted no statement without a clause reference (faithfulness), and IT wanted results in the matter system within an hour of upload (latency). Each became a measurable criterion with an owner, and the "within an hour" item turned out to be an assumption IT had made, not a business need. Options that propose an architecture straight from a vague request ("seamless", "smart") skip discovery. The better option asks the questions that turn the phrase into constraints. A design document that states a retention period, a volume or a latency target with no source is presenting an assumption as fact. The right step is to confirm it.

Discovery questions present stakeholder statements and ask what the requirement is, which item is an assumption, or what to ask next. Use the four questions, translate phrases into measurable constraints, separate what Claude does from rules that belong to systems, and flag anything without a source as an assumption to confirm.
