Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs. Present architectural decisions so stakeholders can act on them, stating what they gain, what they give up and what reversing the decision would cost, in the language of the person deciding.

An architect can understand a trade-off perfectly and still fail to get a decision, because the people deciding do not think in tokens, endpoints or chunking strategies. They need to know what they are choosing between, in terms of the things they are accountable for.

1. What you gain with this option. 2. What you give up : cost, capability, speed, risk. 3. What reversal costs : what it would take to change course after the system is built around this choice. The third element is the one most often left out, and it is what turns apparent agreement into real agreement. A stakeholder who approves an option without knowing it is hard to undo has not really decided. Example decision Gain Give up Reversal cost Load whole documents instead of building retrieval Simpler to build and launch Higher cost per call as documents grow Building retrieval later, under production cost pressure One delivery route for all workloads Simpler identity, logging and operations Flexibility for regional or regulatory needs A late residency requirement can block go-live Lighter logging to save latency A faster experience Visibility into individual decisions Rebuilding audit trails after an incident or audit finding

docs.c: Recommend, but make the choice real
docs.x: Audience Frame the trade-off in terms of Finance Run cost, payback, cost per outcome, budget risk Operations leaders Throughput, SLAs, staff workload, peak capacity Compliance and legal Obligations met or at risk, evidence, liability Executives Business outcome, timing, risk, what is irreversible Engineering Complexity, reliability, maintainability A weak answer to "why can't we use one platform for everything?" lists endpoints and regions. A strong answer says: one platform is cheaper to build and run; it limits our ability to meet different countries' data rules; if such a rule arrives after launch, moving regulated workloads could delay rollout by months. "I recommend choosing the primary platform by our strictest compliance need, and adding a second route only where a workload needs it." Present the options honestly, including the one you would not pick, with all three elements for each. Then give your recommendation and why. A presentation with only one viable option is not a decision.

docs.c: Cheaper, until it is not · Benefits and drawbacks without reversal cost · Technical framing for a business decider
docs.x: A demonstration built on the stakeholder's own scenario, with realistic (anonymized) data, shows more than a generic one. State one or two known limitations up front: discovering them halfway through damages trust, while naming them shows control of the scope. A team proposed dropping prompt caching work to ship a week earlier. Presented as "gain: one week; give up: about $4,000 a month in run cost; reversal: one week of work later, at any time", the sponsor chose to ship early, knowingly. The same team presented "lighter logging for 300 ms faster responses" with its reversal cost, rebuilding the audit trail for a regulated workflow, and the sponsor rejected it. When a question asks what is missing from a trade-off presentation, the answer is often the cost of changing course later. Options that explain the trade-off in implementation detail to a CFO or business sponsor are weaker than ones that state the business consequence.

Trade-off questions describe a decision, an audience and some options. Choose the presentation that states gain, cost and reversal cost in the audience's terms, includes a recommendation, and respects stated requirements (an explicit audit-trail requirement cannot be traded away for speed). Watch for options that omit reversal cost or hide a requirement violation inside a performance gain.

Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs). Turn production signals into decisions through a defined feedback loop, decide which signals reach stakeholders, define SLAs as commitments with breach responses, and keep calendar-based governance checks separate from metric alerts.

Monitoring (lesson 4.5) tells you what is happening. A feedback loop decides what happens next, and who needs to know. Without one, dashboards fill up, alerts are ignored, and stakeholders hear about problems from their customers.

1. Signals: what is the system showing? Metrics, review findings, user feedback, incidents. 2. Triage: what needs attention now, what can wait, what is noise? 3. Decide: does this need an engineering fix, an architect's review, a stakeholder decision, or nothing? 4. Act: fix, adjust a guardrail, escalate, or change scope. 5. Review: did it work? Should the trigger or the rule itself change?

Destination What goes there Example Internal monitoring Routine engineering signals within agreed limits 95th-percentile latency up 50 ms, still under target Architect review Signals that threaten a design assumption or business constraint Evaluation score falling three weeks running; cost per case over budget Stakeholder review Agreed commitments and governance checkpoints SLA breach; scheduled compliance confirmation; scope change Noise Self-resolving or insignificant events One malformed request from a known bad client; a retry that succeeded Escalating everything to stakeholders is as harmful as escalating nothing: it trains them to ignore you. Agree the routing of each signal in advance.

docs.c: Calendar checks run whatever the metrics say
docs.x: A service level agreement states: - the metric (for example, 95th-percentile response time, measured at the gateway), - the threshold and the measurement window (under 3 seconds, per rolling hour), - what counts as a breach (two consecutive hours over threshold), - the response (who is notified, what is done, by when, and what the customer is told). Thresholds come from somewhere tangible: user expectations, business criticality, evaluation criteria, agreed budgets. A number the engineering team picked because it was easy to meet is not an SLA. For AI systems, SLAs often include quality as well as speed: an accuracy floor on the evaluation set, or a maximum escalation rate. Some governance checks are scheduled obligations: a quarterly output audit, an annual residency confirmation, a periodic bias review. They happen on their date even when every metric is green. Threshold triggers and calendar triggers are different things; a good governance plan has both.

docs.c: An alert nobody owned · Waiting for a metric to trigger an audit · Escalating every alert to stakeholders
docs.x: Stakeholders' expectations drift: early demos set a high bar, a good first month sets another, a competitor's announcement sets a third. Keep a shared, written record of what was agreed (criteria, SLAs, known limitations) and review it at a regular cadence, with production evidence. Surprises should come from the world, not from misunderstandings. A document assistant's faithfulness score fell slowly for six weeks. Engineering saw it on a dashboard but treated it as "within noise"; the business sponsor never saw it. When a customer complained, the drop had reached 9 points. Afterwards, the team agreed that any three-week decline over 2 points goes to architect review, and any breach of the 94% floor goes to the sponsor within a day. If a scenario mentions a scheduled compliance review, the correct answer is to hold it on schedule, even when performance is excellent. Options that send routine engineering signals to business stakeholders create fatigue. Route by the agreed triage categories.

These questions describe production signals and ask where each should go, how to define an SLA, or what to do about a scheduled check. Use the loop and the four triage destinations, define SLAs with metric, threshold, breach and response, base thresholds on business needs, and keep calendar-based governance checks separate from metric alerts.

Document architectures and provide implementation guidance. Document architectures so a successor can change them safely and an auditor can verify them, with decision logs that record the rejected options and the reasons, an assumption register, runbooks and a control register.

The architect who designed a system will not run it forever. A successor who inherits diagrams and code but not the reasons will, sooner or later, "simplify" something that was there for a reason: switch to a global endpoint, remove an approval step, drop a log field. Documentation exists to prevent that, and to let auditors check that controls are real.

docs.c: Could a competent stranger change it safely?
docs.x: If an architect who was not involved could read the documentation and make a change without breaking a requirement, it is complete. If they would have to guess why something is the way it is, it is not.

A decision record captures more than the choice: Field Example Decision Use the cloud platform route with the region set explicitly Alternatives rejected The global endpoint; the direct API Trade-off resolved Simpler configuration versus the data-residency obligation Rationale Customer contracts require in-region processing; the global endpoint could route elsewhere Owner Platform lead Evidence Regional configuration export; data-flow record Assumptions The contract requirement covers logs as well (confirmed by legal, March) Revisit when A new region is needed, or the provider changes regional options The rationale and the rejected alternatives are the most valuable fields for a successor, and the ones most often missing.

For the person taking over For the compliance reviewer Explains intent Architecture diagram, decision log, assumption register Control register (obligation, control, owner) Shows evidence Deployment runbook, test and evaluation results Control register with links to evidence Artifact Records Assumption register What is not yet confirmed, and who will confirm it Decision log What was chosen, what was rejected, and why Architecture diagram Components, data flows, trust boundaries Runbook How to deploy, operate, roll back and respond to incidents Evaluation summary What was tested, on what data, with what results Control register Obligations mapped to controls, owners and evidence

Handoffs also go forward , to the team that builds. Give them the requirements with sources, the decisions with rationale, the success criteria and evaluation set, interface contracts (tool definitions, schemas), the prompt templates and their versioning rules, and the non-negotiables ("medication lists are inserted by code, never generated"). For AI systems, prompts, model versions and evaluation sets are part of the design and need the same care as code.

docs.c: The approval step that looked redundant · Diagrams as documentation · Test results as compliance evidence
docs.x: Documentation drifts like configuration. Update the decision log when decisions change, re-date assumptions when confirmed, and plan for known future events, such as a model version being retired, with a note on how to migrate and what to re-evaluate. A new team lead removed the supervisor approval on refunds over $250, reasoning that the assistant "already checks the policy". There was no record that the approval existed because finance auditors required it. The decision log entry, had it existed, would have said: "Rejected: model-only policy check. Reason: finance audit requires named approver for refunds over $250." A diagram shows what exists, not why. Options that consider a diagram plus code "complete documentation" miss the decision rationale. A test summary shows that something was tested once. Compliance reviewers need a control register with current evidence that each control operates.

Documentation questions ask what a handoff package is missing, which artifact serves which audience, or what would have prevented a successor's mistake. The answer is usually the decision log with rationale and rejected alternatives, the assumption register, or the control register with evidence, matched to the audience.

Support lifecycle phases (discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration). Carry requirements through discovery, design, handoff, monitoring and iteration, decide when to iterate and when to re-architect, and gate expansion on documented business outcomes.
An AI solution is not delivered once. It moves through phases, and the architect's job is to make sure what was learned in one phase shapes the next.

Phase Main work Key outputs Discovery Understand goals; translate them into requirements and assumptions Translation table, requirements, assumption register, success criteria Design Choose patterns, models, routes; weigh trade-offs Architecture, decision log, evaluation plan, control register Handoff Transfer the design and its reasons to builders and operators Implementation guidance, runbooks, evaluation set Monitoring Watch signals, SLAs and governance checkpoints Dashboards, governance table, reviews Iteration Improve, fix, extend, or re-architect Changes gated by evaluation; updated documents; outcome measurement The phases connect. A residency requirement found in discovery leads to a regional route in design, a recorded rejection of the global endpoint at handoff, a scheduled residency check in monitoring, and constraints on any performance fix during iteration.

Situation Response Inconsistent output format Iterate on the prompt Retrieval quality slipping Tune chunking, filters or index Cost over budget from bloated context Optimize context and caching Small latency variation within SLA Monitor A new mandatory approval step changes the workflow Re-architect that workflow The chosen route cannot meet a new residency obligation Revisit the deployment architecture A model version is being retired Plan a migration, re-run the evaluation suite, update prompts if needed Diagnose first (lesson 4.4); re-architect only when the cause is structural.

docs.c: Expansion waits for evidence
docs.x: Technical success is not business success. Before expanding a deployment, document the outcome: Field Captures Use case The business problem and its scope boundary Metric before The baseline, measured before deployment Metric after The same metric, measured the same way, after a long enough period Auditable control The evidence that makes the result trustworthy (for example, approval logs) Measurement owner The named person responsible for the measurement Reuse potential Where the solution or its patterns could apply next If the "after" measurement period is too short, do not extrapolate. Confirm the control is working, name the owner, set the date when the measurement will be complete, and hold the expansion decision until then.

docs.c: A pilot that was not ready to scale · Technical metrics as proof of value · Re-architecting for a prompt problem
docs.x: Models are versioned and eventually retired. Pin versions in production, track deprecation notices, and keep the evaluation suite ready so a migration is a planned release, not an emergency. The regression suite is what makes this routine. After four weeks, a sales-proposal assistant had excellent technical metrics, and the sales director wanted to roll it out to all regions. The architect's outcome document showed "time to first draft" had only two weeks of clean data, and win-rate impact (the real goal) would take a quarter to observe. The rollout was approved for one more region, with the full decision scheduled for the end of the quarter. Latency, availability and evaluation scores show the system works. They do not show it delivered the business outcome. Expansion questions want the outcome document. A wording or format issue is fixed by iteration. Options that rebuild the architecture for it are disproportionate.

Lifecycle questions ask which phase an activity belongs to, whether a problem calls for iteration or re-architecture, or whether a deployment is ready to expand. Carry constraints through every phase, diagnose before re-architecting, and gate expansion on an outcome document with a real before-and-after measurement, an auditable control and a named owner.

Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code). Set teams up with a shared, enforced Claude Code configuration, distribute Skills through the mechanism that fits each audience, bound spending up front, and roll out through champions rather than a single big launch.

Giving every engineer access and letting each one configure Claude Code alone produces forty different setups, uneven results and no way to enforce anything. Team setup is an architecture decision with four parts: shared configuration, distribution of reusable assets, spend posture and rollout.

docs.c: Put musts in settings, shoulds in instructions
docs.x: Claude Code reads configuration at several levels, and the difference between them matters. Layer What it does Use for Organization-managed settings Set by administrators; override user and project settings Rules that must hold everywhere: denied commands and paths, allowed tools, approved model choices Project settings (in the repository) Shared by everyone working in that project Project permissions, hooks, MCP servers the project needs Instruction files (CLAUDE.md) at organization, project and user level Load standing context and conventions into every session Coding standards, repository layout, how to run tests User settings Personal preferences Editor habits, personal shortcuts Instruction files are guidance : Claude follows them, but they cannot prevent an action. Permissions, managed settings and hooks are enforcement . Anything that must never happen ("never read .env files", "never push to main") belongs in permission rules or hooks, not only in an instruction file. If breaking a rule would be an incident, enforce it with managed settings, permissions or a hook. Instruction files are for conventions and context.

Mechanism Reaches Versioning and rollback Fits Project Skills in the repository Everyone working in that repository Versioned and rolled back with the repository One team's procedures and conventions Plugins managed for the organization Chosen groups or the whole organization Version-controlled updates; can be required, installed by default or optional Governed procedures and tool sets for specific teams Organization-provisioned Skills Everyone in the organization Central availability, more limited version control Capabilities everyone should have API Skills Your own products, programmatically Version pinning in the calling system Machine-to-machine reuse Choose by who needs it and how much control over updates and rollback you need . A shared asset with no way to roll back can push one bad change to every engineer at once.

Decide the limits before usage grows: default model and allowed models, guidance on effort or thinking levels, per-user and per-team spending caps, rate limits, and usage reporting. Track usage and outcomes with analytics so spending can be tied to results.

docs.c: A rule that was only a suggestion · Security rules in an instruction file only · Big-bang rollout
docs.x: 1. Pilot with a champion in each team , who adapts the shared setup, finds the useful workflows and writes them down. 2. Expand in batches , team by team, with the champion supporting each batch. 3. Measure and adjust : usage, outcomes (cycle time, review findings), costs and feedback, before the next batch. Two failure patterns to avoid: lumpy adoption (a few heavy users, everyone else idle, so practice never standardizes) and stalling at chat (teams use it to ask questions but never adopt repository-aware workflows, Skills or tool integrations, because nobody enabled them). A team's CLAUDE.md said "never modify files under /migrations". After an engineer approved a batch of edits without reading them, a migration file changed. The rule moved into a deny permission in the project settings, plus a hook that blocks any edit to that path, and the instruction file now explains why. Options that rely on CLAUDE.md to stop secret access, destructive commands or protected-branch pushes are weaker than ones that use permissions, managed settings or hooks. "Give everyone access on Monday" is usually wrong in a scenario about adoption. Champions and batches turn access into consistent practice.

Team-configuration questions ask where a rule belongs, which distribution mechanism fits a Skill, how to control spend, or how to roll out. Enforce must-never rules in settings, permissions or hooks; use instruction files for conventions; match distribution to audience and rollback needs; set spend limits up front; and roll out through champions and batches.

Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling. Fit AI assistance into the existing development workflow at the stages where it helps, give Claude ways to verify its own work, and keep a review discipline that ensures people still understand what ships.

The value of AI-assisted development comes from improving the workflow a team already has, not from bolting a chat window beside it. The architect's job is to put assistance where it helps and to keep the quality bar where it was.

Stage How Claude helps What still needs a person Understanding Exploring an unfamiliar codebase, explaining code, tracing a flow Judging whether the explanation is right Planning Proposing an approach and the files to change, before any edit Approving the plan Writing Implementations, tests, boilerplate, refactors from a clear specification Correctness, security and design review Reviewing Summarizing a diff, flagging likely issues, checking conventions in CI The decision to merge Debugging Hypotheses from symptoms, logs and traces Confirming the hypothesis against evidence

docs.h: Practices that make the output better
docs.x: - Explore, then plan, then code. Asking Claude to read the relevant code and propose a plan before editing produces better changes than asking for code straight away. A read-only planning mode helps. - Give it a way to check itself. Tests, a build, a linter, a screenshot to compare against: when Claude can run the check, it can find and fix its own mistakes before a person sees them. - Small, reviewable changes. Large AI-generated diffs are hard to review well. Break work into steps a reviewer can actually read. - Parallel sessions for independent work , each in its own working copy (for example git worktrees), so tasks do not interfere. - Automation in CI. Running Claude non-interactively with structured output lets it review pull requests, triage failures or update documentation as pipeline steps, with deterministic checks (hooks, tests) around it.

docs.c: The author must understand what ships
docs.x: AI makes code cheaper to produce, so more of it reaches review. The bar does not move. A team checklist for any AI-assisted change covers: Dimension The change passes when Correctness Tests cover the requirement and its edge cases, and they pass Security No secrets, inputs validated, least-privilege access for any new calls Maintainability It follows team conventions and introduces no unexplained complexity Understanding The author can explain what it does, why, and how it handles inputs no test covered Passing tests is not the same as understanding. The person who submits a change is accountable for it, whoever or whatever wrote it. The risk the last row guards against is judgment erosion : a team that ships code it no longer understands because it looked right and passed shallow checks, until an input nobody reasoned about reaches production.

docs.c: Faster code, slower reviews · "Tests pass, so it can merge" · AI review as the final verdict
docs.x: Track workflow outcomes, not just usage: pull request cycle time, review rework, escaped defects, time spent on toil. A tool that speeds up writing but slows down review, or raises defects, has not improved the workflow. After adopting AI-assisted coding, a team's pull requests doubled in size and review time per pull request rose by 70%; cycle time barely improved. Splitting work into smaller changes, asking for a plan before code, and requiring authors to annotate non-obvious generated sections brought review time back down and cut cycle time by a third. Options that treat green tests as sufficient for AI-generated code skip the understanding and security checks. The better option keeps the full review bar. An automated review is input to a person's decision, not the decision. Options that let an AI reviewer approve merges on its own are usually wrong.

Workflow questions describe a team using AI tooling and a problem: low quality, slow reviews, unclear ownership, uneven use. Strong answers place assistance at the right stage, give Claude a way to verify its work, keep changes reviewable, keep humans accountable with a verification checklist, and measure workflow outcomes rather than usage.

Support debugging and operational issue resolution. Support teams running Claude systems by connecting symptoms to architectural causes, and leave behind runbooks and escalation paths so the team can resolve the familiar problems without you.

When a Claude-powered system misbehaves, the architect is often the person who knows why. The fast response is to fix it yourself. The lasting response is to fix it with the team and leave behind what they need to fix the next one alone.

Most operational symptoms trace back to a small set of architectural causes. Writing the mapping down is the start of a runbook. Symptom Likely causes First action Quality declined gradually with no code change Model version change, prompt change, retrieval drift as content grew or changed Run the evaluation set; check model, prompt and corpus change history Latency spiked Context grew, a tool slowed down, the cache stopped hitting Read traces for the slowest step; check tokens per request and cache hit rate Intermittent tool failures Expired credentials, rate limits, unhandled error paths Trace one failed call end to end; check auth and limits for that tool Cost rose without more usage Larger tier in use, cache regression, growing context, retry loops Compare model mix, cache hits and tokens per request with the budget model Requests rejected or outputs cut off Context too large; output limit too low Check the error type and stop reasons; count tokens Agent loops or never finishes Missing stopping rule, a tool that keeps failing quietly Read the trace; check turn limits and tool error handling

docs.c: Teach the path, not just the fix
docs.x: A runbook entry records: the symptom as the on-call engineer will see it, how to confirm it, the likely causes in order, the first action for each, how to verify the fix, and when to escalate. Good entries are written after real incidents, tested by someone other than the author, and updated when the system changes. Every incident you resolve should end with a runbook entry the team wrote or reviewed. The goal is a team that needs the architect for new problems, not familiar ones.

People need to know where their responsibility ends. An escalation path names who handles what (first-line on-call, the team owning the AI service, the architect, the platform or vendor) and the conditions for moving up: severity, duration, customer impact, safety or compliance implications. Without it, issues either sit with someone who cannot fix them or go straight to the busiest person.

docs.c: A slow decline no one connected · The architect as permanent firefighter · Changing the model as a first step

An internal knowledge assistant's answer quality slid over a quarter while dashboards stayed green. The cause was a document library that had doubled in size without the index being rebuilt on the new structure. Nobody on the support rota knew that "gradual decline, no code change" points to retrieval drift. After the fix, the team added that runbook entry and a monthly retrieval-recall check; the next drift was caught in a week. In support scenarios, the strongest answer usually combines resolving the issue with building the team's ability to resolve it next time: a runbook entry, an escalation path, a monitoring check. For drift, latency or cost symptoms, the first action is to look at traces and change history. Swapping models first changes a variable before the cause is known.

Support questions describe a symptom and ask for the likely cause, the first action, or how to stop the same problem recurring. Use the symptom-to-cause mapping, start with evidence (traces, change history, evaluation runs), and prefer answers that leave behind a runbook entry and a clear escalation path.

A latency target, an audit need, where data may be stored, a budget or an approved vendor usually rules out two options. 2. Facts come from the system that owns them. Balances and status are fetched with a tool; numbers are computed in code. Claude does the language work. 3. Enforce outside the model. Permissions, limits and approvals live in code and gates, never only in the prompt. 4. Start simple; change on evidence. The simplest pattern, model and prompt that meet the bar, changed only when an evaluation shows a gap. 5. Measure the right thing. The slowest requests under load, cost per successful outcome, and results per group of cases (a "slice"), not one average. 6. Find the cause before the fix. A bigger model is rarely the first answer.

Remember: use the simplest design that works. Claude does the language, systems own the facts, people own the risky decisions. If the question says Pick Not Is this a good job for Claude? A US teaching hospital where physicians spend too long writing discharge summaries, summaries are often incomplete, and every word is protected health information.

Lakeview Regional Medical Center is a 640-bed teaching hospital in Minneapolis, Minnesota, with about 2,900 discharges a month . Every discharge needs a discharge summary: the hospital course, diagnoses, procedures, medications at discharge, results still pending, and follow-up instructions for the patient and their primary care doctor.

- Physicians spend about 2.1 hours a day on documentation; a discharge summary takes 35 minutes on average. - The coding team returns 12% of summaries for missing or unclear information, which delays billing by an average of 4 days . - 1 in 7 discharges is delayed past noon because the summary is not signed.

docs.h: How a discharge summary is written today
docs.x: 1. The physician reads the stay's notes in the electronic health record (EHR): admission note, daily progress notes, consult notes, procedure reports. 2. They write the hospital course and list diagnoses and procedures. 3. They copy the discharge medication list from the pharmacist's medication reconciliation. 4. They check for results that are still pending. 5. They write follow-up instructions and book follow-up appointments. 6. They sign the summary, which is sent to the patient's primary care doctor. 7. Coders assign diagnosis and procedure codes from the signed summary.

A property and auto insurer whose claims intake team keys every new claim by hand, misses its acknowledgement SLA and makes costly keying errors.

Prairie State Mutual, based in Des Moines, Iowa, is a mid-sized property and auto insurer with customers in the United States and the European Union. It receives about 18,000 new claims a month (first notice of loss).

Channel Share What arrives Email 60% A free-text description, often with photos and attachments Web form 30% Structured fields plus uploaded photos and documents Scanned mail 10% Handwritten or printed forms, sometimes with medical reports Fourteen intake handlers read each claim, key 31 fields into ClaimsCore (the claims system of record), check that the policy was active on the date of loss, request any missing documents, and send an acknowledgement to the customer. Measured baseline (last quarter's operations data): - Average handling time: 22 minutes per claim . - Keying errors: 6% of claims have at least one wrong field (from a monthly quality sample of 400 claims).
